It often falls to _The Nation_ to burst the bubble of publicity that surrounds certain new novels widely reviewed and praised in the press. It is one of the magazine’s oldest traditions. A candidate for the most contrarian review of a popular work of fiction would be [Ernest Jones’s withering take on Salinger’s _The Catcher in the Rye_](https://www.scribd.com/doc/271507621/July-16-1951), published on this day in 1951. Jones, a professor of English at Queens College, did not much like the book.

> Echoes reach me of the popularity of _The Catcher in the Rye_. Why has this unpretentious, mildly affecting chronicle of a few days in the life of a disturbed adolescent been read with enthusiasm by Book-of-the-Month Club and lending-library adults ordinarily concerned with fiction as a frivolous diversion or as a source of lofty, incontrovertible platitudes? Entirely, I think, because, like many contemporary and highly praised novels written on the assumption that the mere record of budding sensitiveness automatically results in fiction, the book is a mirror. It reflects something not at all rich and strange but what every sensitive sixteen-year-old since Rousseau has felt, and of course what each one of us is certain he has felt….
> 
> 
> The skill with which all this has been worked into 277 pages is most ingenious. But as it proceeds on its insights, which are not really insights since they are so general, _The Catcher in the Rye_ becomes more and more a case history of all of us. Radically this writing depends on the reader’s recollection of merely similar difficulties; the unique crisis and the unique anguish are not re-created. These emotional ups and downs become increasingly factitious—so much must be included to elicit memories of so many callow heartbreaks—and though always lively in its parts, the book as a whole is predictable and boring.

It often falls to _The Nation_ to burst the bubble of publicity that surrounds certain new novels widely reviewed and praised in the press. It is one of the magazine’s oldest traditions. A candidate for the most contrarian review of a popular work of fiction would be [Ernest Jones’s withering take on Salinger’s _The Catcher in the Rye_](https://www.scribd.com/doc/271507621/July-16-1951), published on this day in 1951. Jones, a professor of English at Queens College, did not much like the book.

> Echoes reach me of the popularity of _The Catcher in the Rye_. Why has this unpretentious, mildly affecting chronicle of a few days in the life of a disturbed adolescent been read with enthusiasm by Book-of-the-Month Club and lending-library adults ordinarily concerned with fiction as a frivolous diversion or as a source of lofty, incontrovertible platitudes? Entirely, I think, because, like many contemporary and highly praised novels written on the assumption that the mere record of budding sensitiveness automatically results in fiction, the book is a mirror. It reflects something not at all rich and strange but what every sensitive sixteen-year-old since Rousseau has felt, and of course what each one of us is certain he has felt….
> 
> 
> The skill with which all this has been worked into 277 pages is most ingenious. But as it proceeds on its insights, which are not really insights since they are so general, _The Catcher in the Rye_ becomes more and more a case history of all of us. Radically this writing depends on the reader’s recollection of merely similar difficulties; the unique crisis and the unique anguish are not re-created. These emotional ups and downs become increasingly factitious—so much must be included to elicit memories of so many callow heartbreaks—and though always lively in its parts, the book as a whole is predictable and boring.

### What is _The Catcher in the Rye_ about?

[J.D. Salinger](https://www.britannica.com/biography/J-D-Salinger)’s novel _The Catcher in the Rye_ (1951) is about a teenage boy, [Holden Caulfield](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Holden-Caulfield), who recounts a few days in his life before the previous [Christmas](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Christmas), including his having been expelled from his[prep school](https://www.britannica.com/topic/preparatory-school). Showcasing his confusion and disillusionment, Holden desperately searches for truth among the “phonies” of the world, which causes him to become increasingly unstable emotionally. The [novel](https://www.britannica.com/art/novel)’s events are related by Holden after the fact from what is implied to be a sanatorium.

### What is the main theme of _The Catcher in the Rye_?

The main theme of [J.D. Salinger](https://www.britannica.com/biography/J-D-Salinger)’s novel _The Catcher in the Rye_ (1951) is the loss of innocence. [Holden Caulfield](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Holden-Caulfield), the book’s teenage narrator, wants to be the “catcher in the rye” (a reference to a poem by [Robert Burns](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Robert-Burns) that Holden misquotes), saving children from falling into adulthood. Other themes in the novel include youthful alienation and grief. Notably, the story takes place a few years after Holden’s younger brother, Allie, has died from [leukemia](https://www.britannica.com/science/leukemia).

### Why was _The Catcher in the Rye_ controversial?

[J.D. Salinger](https://www.britannica.com/biography/J-D-Salinger)’s novel _The Catcher in the Rye_ (1951) has been [banned](https://www.britannica.com/topic/book-banning) numerous times because of its salty language and sexual content. In addition, the [novel](https://www.britannica.com/art/novel) was a favorite of two notorious figures of the late 20th century: [Mark David Chapman](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Mark-David-Chapman), who assassinated musician [John Lennon](https://www.britannica.com/biography/John-Lennon) in 1980, and John Hinckley, Jr., who attempted to assassinate U.S. Pres. [Ronald Reagan](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Ronald-Reagan) in 1981.

**_The Catcher in the Rye_** is a [novel](https://www.britannica.com/art/novel) by American author [J.D. Salinger](https://www.britannica.com/biography/J-D-Salinger) published in 1951. The novel details two days in the life of 16-year-old [Holden Caulfield](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Holden-Caulfield) after he has been expelled from [prep school](https://www.britannica.com/topic/preparatory-school). Confused and [disillusioned](https://www.britannica.com/dictionary/disillusioned), Holden searches for truth and rails against the “phoniness” of the adult world. He ends up exhausted and emotionally unstable. The events are related by Holden after the fact in vivid, humorous language, with a great deal of teenage [slang](https://www.britannica.com/topic/slang). A self-admitted “terrific liar,” Holden is both the quintessential unreliable narrator and a portrait of youthful [alienation](https://www.britannica.com/topic/alienation-society) and grief.

Quick Facts
*   **Title:**_The Catcher in the Rye_ 
*   **Author:**[J.D. Salinger](https://www.britannica.com/biography/J-D-Salinger) 
*   **Published:**July 16, 1951 
*   **Genre:**[Novel](https://www.britannica.com/art/novel) 
*   **Language:**[English](https://www.britannica.com/topic/English-language) 
*   **Quote:** “The thing with kids is, if they want to grab for the gold ring, you have to let them do it, and not say anything. If they fall off, they fall off, but it’s bad if you say anything to them.” 

_The Catcher in the Rye_ is considered to be a classic of 20th-century [American fiction](https://www.britannica.com/art/American-literature). An especially popular choice for [high school](https://www.britannica.com/topic/high-school)[literature](https://www.britannica.com/art/literature) courses, the novel had sold 75 million copies by the early 21st century. Salinger’s storytelling and use of language influenced many other novels told in first-person narration.

## Plot summary and characters

From what is implied to be a sanatorium, Holden tells the story of his adventures before the previous [Christmas](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Christmas). The story begins with Holden at Pencey Prep School on his way to the house of his history teacher, Spencer, so that he can say goodbye. He reveals to the reader that he has been expelled for failing most of his classes. After he visits Spencer, he [encounters](https://www.britannica.com/dictionary/encounters) his roommate, Ward Stradlater, who asks Holden to write an essay for him for English class while he goes on a date with a longtime friend of Holden’s. Having agreed, Holden writes about the [baseball](https://www.britannica.com/sports/baseball) glove of his younger brother, Allie, who died of [leukemia](https://www.britannica.com/science/leukemia). When Stradlater returns, he tells Holden that the essay isn’t good, and Holden gets angry when Stradlater refuses to say whether he had sex with his date. This causes Holden to storm out and leave Pencey for [New York City](https://www.britannica.com/place/New-York-City) a few days earlier than planned for Christmas break.

Once Holden arrives in [New York](https://www.britannica.com/place/New-York-state), he cannot go home, as his parents do not [yet](https://www.britannica.com/dictionary/yet) know that he has been expelled. Instead, he rents a room at the Edmont Hotel, where he witnesses some sexually charged scenes through the windows of other rooms. His loneliness then causes him to seek out human interaction, which he does at the Lavender Room, the hotel’s nightclub. After interacting with some women there, he goes to another nightclub, only to leave after seeing his elder brother’s ex-girlfriend. When he gets back to the hotel, he orders a prostitute to his room, only to talk to her. This situation ends in him being punched in the stomach.

The next morning, Holden calls Sally Hayes, an ex-girlfriend of his. They spend the day together until Holden makes a rude remark and she leaves crying. Holden then meets up with a former schoolmate, Carl Luce, at a bar, but Luce leaves early because he becomes annoyed by Holden’s immature comments. Holden stays behind and gets drunk by himself. After he leaves, he wanders in [Central Park](https://www.britannica.com/place/Central-Park-New-York-City) until the cold drives him to his family’s apartment. He sneaks in, still not prepared to face his parents, and finds his 10-year-old sister, Phoebe. She is upset when she hears that Holden has failed out and accuses him of not liking anything.

[Video 1](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bow-7NORFmI)Holden describes to his sister his fantasy of being “the catcher in the rye,” which was inspired by a song he heard a little boy singing: “If a body catch a body comin’ through the rye.” Phoebe tells him that the words are “If a body _meet_ a body coming through the rye,” from a poem by [Robert Burns](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Robert-Burns). (Burns’s poem, [“Comin thro’ the Rye,”](https://www.poetryfoundation.org/poems/43801/comin-thro-the-rye) exists in several versions, but most render the lines as “Gin a body meet a body / Comin thro’ the rye.”) Soon they hear their parents come home after a night out, and Holden sneaks away. He calls his former English teacher, Mr. Antolini, who tells Holden he can come stay at his apartment. Holden falls asleep on Antolini’s couch and awakes to Antolini stroking his forehead, which Holden interprets as a sexual advance. He immediately excuses himself and heads to [Grand Central Station](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Grand-Central-Station), where he spends the rest of the night.

When he awakes, he goes to Phoebe’s school and leaves a note telling her that he plans to run away and asking her to meet him at a museum during lunch. She arrives with a packed bag and insists on going with him. He tells her no and instead takes her to the [zoo](https://www.britannica.com/dictionary/zoo), where he watches her ride the carousel in the pouring rain. This is where the flashback ends. The novel closes with Holden explaining that he has fallen “sick” but is expected to go to a new school in the fall.

## Interpretation and themes

_The Catcher in the Rye_ takes the loss of innocence as its primary concern. Holden wants to be the “catcher in the rye”—someone who saves children from falling off a cliff, which can be understood as a [metaphor](https://www.britannica.com/art/metaphor) for entering adulthood. As Holden watches Phoebe on the carousel, engaging in childlike behavior, he is so overcome with happiness that he is, as he puts it, “damn near bawling.” By taking her to the zoo, he allows her to maintain her childlike state, thus being a successful “catcher in the rye.” During this time, however, watching her and the other children on the carousel, he has also come to accept that he cannot save everyone: “The thing with kids is, if they want to grab for the gold ring, you have to let them do it, and not say anything. If they fall off, they fall off.”

Holden’s name is also significant: Holden can be read as “hold on,” and Caulfield can be separated into _caul_ and _field_. Holden’s desire is to “hold on” to the protective covering (the [caul](https://www.britannica.com/science/caul)) that encloses the field of innocence (the same field he wishes to keep the children from leaving). Holden desperately wants to remain true and innocent in a world full of, as he puts it, “phonies.”

Holden is often held up by critics as a classic example of teenage alienation. His use of [sarcasm](https://www.britannica.com/topic/sarcasm) and [slang](https://www.britannica.com/dictionary/slang) are seen as being representative of a phase that many young people go through as they transition to adulthood. However, his behavior is also typical of someone who is grieving, which Holden is: His younger brother, Allie, has only recently died, on July 18, 1946. “You’d have liked him,” Holden says. “He was two years younger than I was, but he was about fifty times as intelligent.” Holden’s idealization of his dead brother is another example of his attempt to hold on to innocence.

Holden’s emotional state is also understood to make him unreliable as a narrator. Ironically, he tells the reader as much, although he couches it by bragging about his habit of lying:

> I’m the most terrific liar you ever saw in your life. It’s awful. If I’m on the way to the store to buy a magazine, even, and somebody asks me where I’m going, I’m [liable](https://www.britannica.com/dictionary/liable) to say I’m going to the opera. It’s terrible.

## Publication, initial reception, and similarities to Salinger’s life

[![Image 21: J.D. Salinger](https://cdn.britannica.com/83/8583-050-06FE3090/J-D-Salinger.jpg?w=300)](https://cdn.britannica.com/83/8583-050-06FE3090/J-D-Salinger.jpg)

[J.D. Salinger](https://cdn.britannica.com/83/8583-050-06FE3090/J-D-Salinger.jpg)Salinger shared several similarities with his characters, including Holden Caulfield, the angsty, grieving teenage narrator of his novel _The Catcher in the Rye_ (1951).(more)

The Caulfield family was one Salinger had already explored in a number of stories that had been published by different magazines. Holden appeared in some of those stories, even narrating one, but he was not as richly fleshed out in them as he would be in _The Catcher in the Rye_. Notably, the sole story that Holden narrates, titled “I’m Crazy” and published in _Collier’s_ in 1945, was written shortly after Salinger’s release from a military hospital, where he had been treated for “combat fatigue” ([post-traumatic stress disorder](https://www.britannica.com/science/post-traumatic-stress-disorder)). Salinger’s experience in the army during [World War II](https://www.britannica.com/event/World-War-II) had included fighting in the [invasion of Normandy on D-Day](https://www.britannica.com/event/Normandy-Invasion). The war and [mental illness](https://www.britannica.com/science/mental-disorder) are recurring themes in many of his works. Moreover, Salinger once admitted in an interview that _The Catcher in the Rye_ was semi-autobiographical.

The novel, unlike the other stories of the Caulfield family, had difficulties getting published. Originally solicited by Harcourt, Brace and Company, the manuscript was rejected after the head of the trade division asked whether Holden was supposed to be crazy. Then Salinger’s agent, Dorothy Olding, approached Little, Brown and Company, which published the novel in 1951. After Little, Brown bought the manuscript, Salinger showed it to _[The New Yorker](https://www.britannica.com/topic/The-New-Yorker)_, assuming that the magazine, which had published several of his [short stories](https://www.britannica.com/art/short-story), would want to print excerpts from the novel. _The New Yorker_ rejected it, however, as the editors found the Caulfield children too [precocious](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/precocious) to be plausible and Salinger’s writing style exhibitionistic.

_The Catcher in the Rye_’s reception was lukewarm at first. Many critics were impressed by Holden as a character and, specifically, by his style of narration. Salinger was able to create a character whose relatability stemmed from his unreliability—something that [resonated](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/resonated) with many readers. _[Time](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Time-American-magazine)_’s reviewer wrote, “[Salinger] charts the miseries and ecstasies of an adolescent rebel, and deals out some of the most acidly humorous deadpan satire since the late great [Ring Lardner](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Ring-Lardner).…He can understand the adolescent mind without displaying one.”

Others, however, felt that the novel was amateur and unnecessarily coarse. In _[The New Republic](https://www.britannica.com/topic/The-New-Republic)_, Anne L. Goodman wrote, “Holden Caulfield…is an extraordinary portrait, but there is too much of him.”

## Legacy

After publishing _The Catcher in the Rye_, Salinger became a recluse. When asked for the rights to adapt it for [Broadway](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Broadway-street-and-district-New-York-City) or [Hollywood](https://www.britannica.com/place/Hollywood-California), he emphatically declined. Despite Holden’s never having appeared in any form subsequent to that in Salinger’s novel, the character has had a long-lasting influence, reaching millions of readers, including two particularly [notorious](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/notorious) ones. In 1980 [Mark David Chapman](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Mark-David-Chapman) identified so wholly with Holden that he became convinced that murdering [John Lennon](https://www.britannica.com/biography/John-Lennon) would turn him into the novel’s protagonist. [John W. Hinckley, Jr.](https://www.britannica.com/biography/John-W-Hinckley-Jr), the attempted assassin of U.S. Pres. [Ronald Reagan](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Ronald-Reagan) in 1981, was also a fan of the novel.

Many critics see evidence of Salinger’s influence (especially Holden’s voice) in such works as Sylvia Plath’s autobiographical novel _[The Bell Jar](https://www.britannica.com/topic/The-Bell-Jar)_ (1963) and [Dave Eggers](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Dave-Eggers)’s memoir _A Heartbreaking Work of Staggering Genius_ (2000). Salinger’s novel also plays an important role in [John Guare](https://www.britannica.com/biography/John-Guare)’s acclaimed play _Six Degrees of Separation_ (1990).

The novel has been banned numerous times because of its salty language and sexual content, although it has remained influential and widely read into the 21st century.

### What is J.D. Salinger famous for?

American author [J.D. Salinger](https://www.britannica.com/biography/J-D-Salinger) (1919–2010) is best known for his novel _The Catcher in the Rye_ (1951), which won critical acclaim and gained a devoted following, particularly among post-[World War II](https://www.britannica.com/event/World-War-II) college students. The novel concerns a teenage boy, [Holden Caulfield](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Holden-Caulfield), and his quest for innocence and truth. After its publication, Salinger became a recluse. He published a few more short stories and books, mostly about the fictional Glass family. The last of these, a [novella](https://www.britannica.com/art/novella) titled _Hapworth 16, 1924_, appeared in _[The New Yorker](https://www.britannica.com/topic/The-New-Yorker)_ in 1965.

### Did J.D. Salinger have PTSD?

During his service in [World War II](https://www.britannica.com/event/World-War-II), American author [J.D. Salinger](https://www.britannica.com/biography/J-D-Salinger) was treated for “[battle fatigue](https://www.britannica.com/science/combat-fatigue),” which is now typically diagnosed as [post-traumatic stress disorder](https://www.britannica.com/science/post-traumatic-stress-disorder) (PTSD). Salinger served in the U.S. Army as a [counterintelligence](https://www.britannica.com/topic/counterintelligence) agent, but his first experience with combat was on D-Day (June 6, 1944), when he participated in the [Normandy landings](https://www.britannica.com/event/Normandy-Invasion) on [Utah Beach](https://www.britannica.com/place/Utah-Beach). He also fought in the [Battle of the Bulge](https://www.britannica.com/event/Battle-of-the-Bulge) and participated in the liberation of a [concentration camp](https://www.britannica.com/topic/concentration-camp) in Germany.

### How did J.D. Salinger’s experience in World War II influence his writing?

[J.D. Salinger](https://www.britannica.com/biography/J-D-Salinger)’s experience in the U.S. Army during [World War II](https://www.britannica.com/event/World-War-II) influenced many elements in his [short stories](https://www.britannica.com/art/short-story). For example, “For Esmé—with Love and Squalor” (1950) describes a U.S. soldier’s poignant encounter with two British children. “A Perfect Day for Bananafish” (1948) concerns the [suicide](https://www.britannica.com/topic/suicide) of the sensitive, despairing veteran Seymour Glass.

### Why did J.D. Salinger become a recluse?

American author [J.D. Salinger](https://www.britannica.com/biography/J-D-Salinger) (1919–2010) became a recluse after the success of his novel _The Catcher in the Rye_ (1951), seeking to escape fame and preserve his privacy. In 1953 he moved from New York City to Cornish, New Hampshire, and rarely engaged with the media or fans to the end of his life.

**J.D. Salinger** (born January 1, 1919, [Manhattan](https://www.britannica.com/place/Manhattan-New-York-City), [New York](https://www.britannica.com/place/New-York-state), U.S.—died January 27, 2010, Cornish, New Hampshire) was an American writer whose [novel](https://www.britannica.com/art/novel)_The Catcher in the Rye_ (1951) won critical acclaim and devoted admirers, especially among the post-[World War II](https://www.britannica.com/event/World-War-II) generation of college students. His corpus of published works also consists of [short stories](https://www.britannica.com/art/short-story) that were printed in magazines, including _The Saturday Evening Post_, _[Esquire](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Esquire-American-magazine)_, and _[The New Yorker](https://www.britannica.com/topic/The-New-Yorker)_. After the success of _The Catcher in the Rye_, Salinger became a recluse. His last published work was a short story in 1965, but he remained an enormously influential figure in contemporary [American literature](https://www.britannica.com/art/American-literature).

## Early life and education

Salinger was the son of a Jewish father, Sol Salinger, and a Scotch-Irish Christian mother, Miriam Salinger (née Marie Jillich). He had an older sister, Doris. Like [Holden Caulfield](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Holden-Caulfield), the hero of _The Catcher in the Rye_, Salinger grew up in [New York City](https://www.britannica.com/place/New-York-City). He attended public schools until his parents enrolled him in McBurney School, an [exclusive](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/exclusive) Manhattan [prep school](https://www.britannica.com/topic/preparatory-school), in the ninth grade. After he failed (also like Holden), his parents sent him to Valley Forge Military Academy in Pennsylvania, which became the model for Pencey Prep in _The Catcher in the Rye_. At [Valley Forge](https://www.britannica.com/place/Valley-Forge-historical-area) his plans to become a writer solidified; he served as literary editor of the school yearbook. His other activities there included managing the school’s [fencing](https://www.britannica.com/sports/fencing) team—another similarity he shared with Holden Caulfield.

After brief periods at [New York](https://www.britannica.com/topic/New-York-University) and [Columbia](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Columbia-University) universities, Salinger devoted himself entirely to writing, and his stories began to appear in periodicals in 1940. The next year he had a [brief career as a cruise ship entertainment director](https://www.britannica.com/topic/List-of-Day-Jobs-of-Famous-Writers).

## Wartime experiences

During [World War II](https://www.britannica.com/event/World-War-II), J.D. Salinger’s first time in combat was in Normandy on D-Day (June 6, 1944).

In 1942 Salinger was [drafted](https://www.britannica.com/dictionary/drafted) into the U.S. Army. Proficient in French and German, he served as a [counterintelligence](https://www.britannica.com/topic/counterintelligence) agent in the 4th Infantry Division and was tasked with interviewing prisoners-of-war, [Nazi](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Nazi-Party) sympathizers, and military deserters. Two years later Salinger participated in the [Normandy landings](https://www.britannica.com/event/Normandy-Invasion) on [Utah Beach](https://www.britannica.com/place/Utah-Beach) on D-Day (June 6, 1944). It was his first time in combat.

Later, Salinger fought in the [Battle of the Bulge](https://www.britannica.com/event/Battle-of-the-Bulge) and participated in the liberation of the [concentration camp](https://www.britannica.com/topic/concentration-camp) at Kaufering, Germany, a subcamp of [Dachau](https://www.britannica.com/place/Dachau-concentration-camp-Germany). While in Europe he met [Ernest Hemingway](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Ernest-Hemingway), who was working as a war correspondent and encouraged Salinger in his writing. However, the war seriously affected the young writer’s health. For several weeks he was hospitalized while being treated for “[battle fatigue](https://www.britannica.com/science/combat-fatigue)” ([post-traumatic stress disorder](https://www.britannica.com/science/post-traumatic-stress-disorder)). During his recovery he wrote a story titled “I’m Crazy,” which was narrated by a teenage character named Holden Caulfield. It was not the first time Holden appeared in one of Salinger’s stories, but it was the first story in which he served as the narrator. “I’m Crazy” was published in December 1945 in _Collier’s_.

_[(Read about other writers who went to war in Britannica’s article “War Stories.”)](https://www.britannica.com/art/War-Stories-13-Modern-Writers-Who-Served-in-War)_

## Literary fame with _The Catcher in the Rye_ and a life in seclusion

After Salinger’s return to the [United States](https://www.britannica.com/place/United-States) (he was honorably discharged in 1946), his name and writing style became increasingly associated with _[The New Yorker](https://www.britannica.com/topic/The-New-Yorker)_ magazine, which published almost all of his later stories. Some of the best of these made use of his wartime experiences: “For Esmé—with Love and Squalor” (1950) describes a U.S. soldier’s [poignant](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/poignant) encounter with two British children, and “A Perfect Day for Bananafish” (1948) concerns the [suicide](https://www.britannica.com/topic/suicide) of the sensitive, despairing veteran Seymour Glass.

[Cover of _The Catcher in the Rye_](https://cdn.britannica.com/94/181394-050-2F76F7EE/Reproduction-cover-edition-The-Catcher-in-the.jpg)Reproduction of the cover of the first edition of J.D. Salinger's novel _The Catcher in the Rye_ (1951).(more)

Major critical and popular recognition came with the publication of _The Catcher in the Rye_, whose central character, the sensitive, rebellious Holden Caulfield, relates in authentic teenage [idiom](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/idiom) his flight from the “phony” adult world, his search for innocence and truth, and his final collapse on a psychiatrist’s couch. The humor and colorful language of _The Catcher in the Rye_ place it in the tradition of [Mark Twain](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Mark-Twain)’s _[Adventures of Huckleberry Finn](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Adventures-of-Huckleberry-Finn-novel-by-Twain)_ and the stories of [Ring Lardner](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Ring-Lardner), but its hero, like most of Salinger’s child characters, views his life with an added dimension of [precocious](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/precocious) self-consciousness.

_The Catcher in the Rye_ made Salinger into a literary celebrity. In an attempt to escape fame and recover the loss of his privacy, he moved from New York to Cornish, [New Hampshire](https://www.britannica.com/place/New-Hampshire-state), in 1953 and went into seclusion. To the end of his life Salinger rarely spoke to the media or engaged with his many fans.

For a while, he continued to publish new work. _Nine Stories_ (1953), a selection of Salinger’s short stories, added to his literary reputation. Several pieces in the collection, which includes “A Perfect Day for Bananafish,” feature the siblings of the fictional [Glass family](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Glass-family). In works such as _[Franny and Zooey](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Franny-and-Zooey)_ (1961) and _Raise High the Roof Beam, Carpenters and Seymour: An Introduction_ (1963), the introspective Glass children, influenced by their eldest brother Seymour and his death, navigate questions about [spirituality](https://www.britannica.com/topic/spirituality) and enlightenment. Similar to _The Catcher in the Rye_, all three books were best-sellers.

## Personal life and later years

The reclusive habits of Salinger in his later years made his personal life a matter of speculation among devotees. According to family members, Salinger’s life in seclusion reflected the quest for spiritual enlightenment of his characters in _Raise High the Roof Beam_. He developed interests in [homeopathic](https://www.britannica.com/science/homeopathy) medicine and [acupuncture](https://www.britannica.com/science/acupuncture), Eastern religions such as [Buddhism](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Buddhism) and [Hinduism](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Hinduism), and [Christian Science](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Christian-Science) and [Scientology](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Scientology). Many critics think Salinger’s [esoteric](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/esoteric) interests were fueled by the trauma of his war experiences.

Salinger was married three times. In 1945 he wed Sylvia Welter, a German woman whom he met in Europe and about whom little else is known. Their marriage lasted eight months. In 1955 he married Claire Douglas, a 19-year-old student at Radcliffe College; they had two children, Margaret and Matthew, before divorcing in 1967.

He subsequently had relationships with several other women, including writer Joyce Maynard, an 18-year-old student at [Yale University](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Yale-University). In April 1972 she had published an [essay in _The New York Times Magazine_](https://archive.nytimes.com/www.nytimes.com/books/98/09/13/specials/maynard-mag.html) that had impressed him—or perhaps, her youthful appearance in the essay’s accompanying photograph did. Salinger, then 53 years old, wrote to her, and they began a correspondence that led to Maynard dropping out of school and moving in with him. After 10 months they broke up, and Maynard returned to Yale. In 1998 she published _At Home in the World_, a memoir of their relationship. The following year she auctioned off his letters. Salinger made no public comment, but he privately accused Maynard of [exploiting](https://www.britannica.com/dictionary/exploiting) him.

In the late 1980s Salinger married Colleen O’Neill, a nurse who is believed to have been about 40 years younger than him.

Meanwhile, his small literary output was a subject of controversy among critics. The last work Salinger published during his lifetime was a [novella](https://www.britannica.com/art/novella) titled _Hapworth 16, 1924_, which appeared in _The New Yorker_ in 1965. It concerns the childhood of Seymour Glass and a letter he writes to his family from [summer camp](https://www.britannica.com/topic/summer-camp). In 1997 Salinger consented to a publisher’s plans to release _Hapworth 16, 1924_ as a book, but he suddenly withdrew his support, scuttling its publication.

“It’s clear he wasn’t so crazy about the splashy aspects of publishing on a certain scale…But I don’t think he ever could strike that balance between the public and private worlds of writing and publishing his work.”—Dave Eggers on Salinger, in _The New Yorker_, 2010

In 1974 _The Complete Uncollected Short Stories of J.D. Salinger_, an unauthorized two-volume work of his early pieces, was briefly released to the public, but sales were halted when Salinger filed a lawsuit for [copyright](https://www.britannica.com/topic/copyright) infringement. Salinger also sued to stop the publication of a biography of him by Ian Hamilton and an unauthorized sequel to _The Catcher in the Rye_. The biography was rewritten and published in 1988 under the title _In Search of J.D. Salinger_. The sequel, _60 Years Later: Coming Through the Rye_, by John David California (a pseudonym of the Swedish writer Fredrik Colting), was published in Britain in 2009, but a judge barred its publication in the United States.

Other unauthorized works about Salinger include _Dream Catcher_ (2000), a memoir by his daughter that claimed he had been abusive to his second wife. She also chronicled his esoteric beliefs and wrote that his personal habits included [arcane](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/arcane) health practices such as drinking his own urine. Salinger’s son, however, has disputed his sister’s account.

## Death and legacy

Salinger died of natural causes in 2010 at age 91. After his death his literary agents released a statement that read in part,

> Salinger had remarked that he was in this world but not of it. His body is gone but the family hopes that he is still with those he loves, whether they are religious or historical figures, personal friends or fictional characters.

Three years later David Shields and Shane Salerno published _Salinger_, a best-selling biography that claimed the writer had several unpublished works that would eventually be released. Others in the literary world had also made such claims; Maynard believed Salinger had the manuscripts for at least two novels locked in a safe at his home. Many people speculated that he had written several volumes about the Glass family. However, no new works were forthcoming.

Salinger’s influence on writers of the latter half of the 20th century and early 21st century was immense. His literary voice was characterized by its humor, [irony](https://www.britannica.com/art/irony), and a pitch-perfect use of [colloquial](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/colloquial) speech. Among those whose work he influenced are [Sylvia Plath](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Sylvia-Plath), [Philip Roth](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Philip-Roth), [Harold Brodkey](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Harold-Brodkey), [John Updike](https://www.britannica.com/biography/John-Updike), and [Dave Eggers](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Dave-Eggers). After Salinger’s death, Eggers memorialized him in an [essay in _The New Yorker_](https://www.newyorker.com/books/page-turner/remembering-salinger-dave-eggers). He wrote,

> His is still my favorite [dialogue](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/dialogue), the dialogue that rings truest, that’s at once very naturalistic and musical…The man was an artist, no doubt about it, and his work was always growing in new—darker, stranger, more wonderfully obsessive—directions. And always, no matter where the stories go (or don’t go), his sentences are so beautiful, and so unlike anyone else’s.

### What is _The Catcher in the Rye_ about?

[J.D. Salinger](https://www.britannica.com/biography/J-D-Salinger)’s novel _The Catcher in the Rye_ (1951) is about a teenage boy, [Holden Caulfield](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Holden-Caulfield), who recounts a few days in his life before the previous [Christmas](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Christmas), including his having been expelled from his[prep school](https://www.britannica.com/topic/preparatory-school). Showcasing his confusion and disillusionment, Holden desperately searches for truth among the “phonies” of the world, which causes him to become increasingly unstable emotionally. The [novel](https://www.britannica.com/art/novel)’s events are related by Holden after the fact from what is implied to be a sanatorium.

### What is the main theme of _The Catcher in the Rye_?

The main theme of [J.D. Salinger](https://www.britannica.com/biography/J-D-Salinger)’s novel _The Catcher in the Rye_ (1951) is the loss of innocence. [Holden Caulfield](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Holden-Caulfield), the book’s teenage narrator, wants to be the “catcher in the rye” (a reference to a poem by [Robert Burns](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Robert-Burns) that Holden misquotes), saving children from falling into adulthood. Other themes in the novel include youthful alienation and grief. Notably, the story takes place a few years after Holden’s younger brother, Allie, has died from [leukemia](https://www.britannica.com/science/leukemia).

### Why was _The Catcher in the Rye_ controversial?

[J.D. Salinger](https://www.britannica.com/biography/J-D-Salinger)’s novel _The Catcher in the Rye_ (1951) has been [banned](https://www.britannica.com/topic/book-banning) numerous times because of its salty language and sexual content. In addition, the [novel](https://www.britannica.com/art/novel) was a favorite of two notorious figures of the late 20th century: [Mark David Chapman](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Mark-David-Chapman), who assassinated musician [John Lennon](https://www.britannica.com/biography/John-Lennon) in 1980, and John Hinckley, Jr., who attempted to assassinate U.S. Pres. [Ronald Reagan](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Ronald-Reagan) in 1981.

**_The Catcher in the Rye_** is a [novel](https://www.britannica.com/art/novel) by American author [J.D. Salinger](https://www.britannica.com/biography/J-D-Salinger) published in 1951. The novel details two days in the life of 16-year-old [Holden Caulfield](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Holden-Caulfield) after he has been expelled from [prep school](https://www.britannica.com/topic/preparatory-school). Confused and [disillusioned](https://www.britannica.com/dictionary/disillusioned), Holden searches for truth and rails against the “phoniness” of the adult world. He ends up exhausted and emotionally unstable. The events are related by Holden after the fact in vivid, humorous language, with a great deal of teenage [slang](https://www.britannica.com/topic/slang). A self-admitted “terrific liar,” Holden is both the quintessential unreliable narrator and a portrait of youthful [alienation](https://www.britannica.com/topic/alienation-society) and grief.

Salinger’s storytelling and use of language influenced many other novels told in first-person narration.

## Plot summary and characters

From what is implied to be a sanatorium, Holden tells the story of his adventures before the previous [Christmas](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Christmas). The story begins with Holden at Pencey Prep School on his way to the house of his history teacher, Spencer, so that he can say goodbye. He reveals to the reader that he has been expelled for failing most of his classes. After he visits Spencer, he [encounters](https://www.britannica.com/dictionary/encounters) his roommate, Ward Stradlater, who asks Holden to write an essay for him for English class while he goes on a date with a longtime friend of Holden’s. Having agreed, Holden writes about the [baseball](https://www.britannica.com/sports/baseball) glove of his younger brother, Allie, who died of [leukemia](https://www.britannica.com/science/leukemia). When Stradlater returns, he tells Holden that the essay isn’t good, and Holden gets angry when Stradlater refuses to say whether he had sex with his date. This causes Holden to storm out and leave Pencey for [New York City](https://www.britannica.com/place/New-York-City) a few days earlier than planned for Christmas break.

Once Holden arrives in [New York](https://www.britannica.com/place/New-York-state), he cannot go home, as his parents do not [yet](https://www.britannica.com/dictionary/yet) know that he has been expelled. Instead, he rents a room at the Edmont Hotel, where he witnesses some sexually charged scenes through the windows of other rooms. His loneliness then causes him to seek out human interaction, which he does at the Lavender Room, the hotel’s nightclub. After interacting with some women there, he goes to another nightclub, only to leave after seeing his elder brother’s ex-girlfriend. When he gets back to the hotel, he orders a prostitute to his room, only to talk to her. This situation ends in him being punched in the stomach.

The next morning, Holden calls Sally Hayes, an ex-girlfriend of his. They spend the day together until Holden makes a rude remark and she leaves crying. Holden then meets up with a former schoolmate, Carl Luce, at a bar, but Luce leaves early because he becomes annoyed by Holden’s immature comments. Holden stays behind and gets drunk by himself. After he leaves, he wanders in [Central Park](https://www.britannica.com/place/Central-Park-New-York-City) until the cold drives him to his family’s apartment. He sneaks in, still not prepared to face his parents, and finds his 10-year-old sister, Phoebe. She is upset when she hears that Holden has failed out and accuses him of not liking anything.

[Video 1](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bow-7NORFmI)Holden describes to his sister his fantasy of being “the catcher in the rye,” which was inspired by a song he heard a little boy singing: “If a body catch a body comin’ through the rye.” Phoebe tells him that the words are “If a body _meet_ a body coming through the rye,” from a poem by [Robert Burns](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Robert-Burns). (Burns’s poem, [“Comin thro’ the Rye,”](https://www.poetryfoundation.org/poems/43801/comin-thro-the-rye) exists in several versions, but most render the lines as “Gin a body meet a body / Comin thro’ the rye.”) Soon they hear their parents come home after a night out, and Holden sneaks away. He calls his former English teacher, Mr. Antolini, who tells Holden he can come stay at his apartment. Holden falls asleep on Antolini’s couch and awakes to Antolini stroking his forehead, which Holden interprets as a sexual advance. He immediately excuses himself and heads to [Grand Central Station](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Grand-Central-Station), where he spends the rest of the night.

When he awakes, he goes to Phoebe’s school and leaves a note telling her that he plans to run away and asking her to meet him at a museum during lunch. She arrives with a packed bag and insists on going with him. He tells her no and instead takes her to the [zoo](https://www.britannica.com/dictionary/zoo), where he watches her ride the carousel in the pouring rain. This is where the flashback ends. The novel closes with Holden explaining that he has fallen “sick” but is expected to go to a new school in the fall.

## Interpretation and themes

_The Catcher in the Rye_ takes the loss of innocence as its primary concern. Holden wants to be the “catcher in the rye”—someone who saves children from falling off a cliff, which can be understood as a [metaphor](https://www.britannica.com/art/metaphor) for entering adulthood. As Holden watches Phoebe on the carousel, engaging in childlike behavior, he is so overcome with happiness that he is, as he puts it, “damn near bawling.” By taking her to the zoo, he allows her to maintain her childlike state, thus being a successful “catcher in the rye.” During this time, however, watching her and the other children on the carousel, he has also come to accept that he cannot save everyone: “The thing with kids is, if they want to grab for the gold ring, you have to let them do it, and not say anything. If they fall off, they fall off.”

Holden’s name is also significant: Holden can be read as “hold on,” and Caulfield can be separated into _caul_ and _field_. Holden’s desire is to “hold on” to the protective covering (the [caul](https://www.britannica.com/science/caul)) that encloses the field of innocence (the same field he wishes to keep the children from leaving). Holden desperately wants to remain true and innocent in a world full of, as he puts it, “phonies.”

Holden is often held up by critics as a classic example of teenage alienation. His use of [sarcasm](https://www.britannica.com/topic/sarcasm) and [slang](https://www.britannica.com/dictionary/slang) are seen as being representative of a phase that many young people go through as they transition to adulthood. However, his behavior is also typical of someone who is grieving, which Holden is: His younger brother, Allie, has only recently died, on July 18, 1946. “You’d have liked him,” Holden says. “He was two years younger than I was, but he was about fifty times as intelligent.” Holden’s idealization of his dead brother is another example of his attempt to hold on to innocence.

Holden’s emotional state is also understood to make him unreliable as a narrator. Ironically, he tells the reader as much, although he couches it by bragging about his habit of lying:

> I’m the most terrific liar you ever saw in your life. It’s awful. If I’m on the way to the store to buy a magazine, even, and somebody asks me where I’m going, I’m [liable](https://www.britannica.com/dictionary/liable) to say I’m going to the opera. It’s terrible.

## Publication, initial reception, and similarities to Salinger’s life

[![Image 21: J.D. Salinger](https://cdn.britannica.com/83/8583-050-06FE3090/J-D-Salinger.jpg?w=300)](https://cdn.britannica.com/83/8583-050-06FE3090/J-D-Salinger.jpg)

[J.D. Salinger](https://cdn.britannica.com/83/8583-050-06FE3090/J-D-Salinger.jpg)Salinger shared several similarities with his characters, including Holden Caulfield, the angsty, grieving teenage narrator of his novel _The Catcher in the Rye_ (1951).(more)

The Caulfield family was one Salinger had already explored in a number of stories that had been published by different magazines. Holden appeared in some of those stories, even narrating one, but he was not as richly fleshed out in them as he would be in _The Catcher in the Rye_. Notably, the sole story that Holden narrates, titled “I’m Crazy” and published in _Collier’s_ in 1945, was written shortly after Salinger’s release from a military hospital, where he had been treated for “combat fatigue” ([post-traumatic stress disorder](https://www.britannica.com/science/post-traumatic-stress-disorder)). Salinger’s experience in the army during [World War II](https://www.britannica.com/event/World-War-II) had included fighting in the [invasion of Normandy on D-Day](https://www.britannica.com/event/Normandy-Invasion). The war and [mental illness](https://www.britannica.com/science/mental-disorder) are recurring themes in many of his works. Moreover, Salinger once admitted in an interview that _The Catcher in the Rye_ was semi-autobiographical.

The novel, unlike the other stories of the Caulfield family, had difficulties getting published. Originally solicited by Harcourt, Brace and Company, the manuscript was rejected after the head of the trade division asked whether Holden was supposed to be crazy. Then Salinger’s agent, Dorothy Olding, approached Little, Brown and Company, which published the novel in 1951. After Little, Brown bought the manuscript, Salinger showed it to _[The New Yorker](https://www.britannica.com/topic/The-New-Yorker)_, assuming that the magazine, which had published several of his [short stories](https://www.britannica.com/art/short-story), would want to print excerpts from the novel. _The New Yorker_ rejected it, however, as the editors found the Caulfield children too [precocious](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/precocious) to be plausible and Salinger’s writing style exhibitionistic.

_The Catcher in the Rye_’s reception was lukewarm at first. Many critics were impressed by Holden as a character and, specifically, by his style of narration. Salinger was able to create a character whose relatability stemmed from his unreliability—something that [resonated](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/resonated) with many readers. _[Time](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Time-American-magazine)_’s reviewer wrote, “[Salinger] charts the miseries and ecstasies of an adolescent rebel, and deals out some of the most acidly humorous deadpan satire since the late great [Ring Lardner](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Ring-Lardner).…He can understand the adolescent mind without displaying one.”

Others, however, felt that the novel was amateur and unnecessarily coarse. In _[The New Republic](https://www.britannica.com/topic/The-New-Republic)_, Anne L. Goodman wrote, “Holden Caulfield…is an extraordinary portrait, but there is too much of him.”

## Legacy

After publishing _The Catcher in the Rye_, Salinger became a recluse. When asked for the rights to adapt it for [Broadway](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Broadway-street-and-district-New-York-City) or [Hollywood](https://www.britannica.com/place/Hollywood-California), he emphatically declined. Despite Holden’s never having appeared in any form subsequent to that in Salinger’s novel, the character has had a long-lasting influence, reaching millions of readers, including two particularly [notorious](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/notorious) ones. In 1980 [Mark David Chapman](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Mark-David-Chapman) identified so wholly with Holden that he became convinced that murdering [John Lennon](https://www.britannica.com/biography/John-Lennon) would turn him into the novel’s protagonist. [John W. Hinckley, Jr.](https://www.britannica.com/biography/John-W-Hinckley-Jr), the attempted assassin of U.S. Pres. [Ronald Reagan](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Ronald-Reagan) in 1981, was also a fan of the novel.

Many critics see evidence of Salinger’s influence (especially Holden’s voice) in such works as Sylvia Plath’s autobiographical novel _[The Bell Jar](https://www.britannica.com/topic/The-Bell-Jar)_ (1963) and [Dave Eggers](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Dave-Eggers)’s memoir _A Heartbreaking Work of Staggering Genius_ (2000). Salinger’s novel also plays an important role in [John Guare](https://www.britannica.com/biography/John-Guare)’s acclaimed play _Six Degrees of Separation_ (1990).

The novel has been banned numerous times because of its salty language and sexual content, although it has remained influential and widely read into the 21st century.

### What is J.D. Salinger famous for?

American author [J.D. Salinger](https://www.britannica.com/biography/J-D-Salinger) (1919–2010) is best known for his novel _The Catcher in the Rye_ (1951), which won critical acclaim and gained a devoted following, particularly among post-[World War II](https://www.britannica.com/event/World-War-II) college students. The novel concerns a teenage boy, [Holden Caulfield](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Holden-Caulfield), and his quest for innocence and truth. After its publication, Salinger became a recluse. He published a few more short stories and books, mostly about the fictional Glass family. The last of these, a [novella](https://www.britannica.com/art/novella) titled _Hapworth 16, 1924_, appeared in _[The New Yorker](https://www.britannica.com/topic/The-New-Yorker)_ in 1965.

### Did J.D. Salinger have PTSD?

During his service in [World War II](https://www.britannica.com/event/World-War-II), American author [J.D. Salinger](https://www.britannica.com/biography/J-D-Salinger) was treated for “[battle fatigue](https://www.britannica.com/science/combat-fatigue),” which is now typically diagnosed as [post-traumatic stress disorder](https://www.britannica.com/science/post-traumatic-stress-disorder) (PTSD). Salinger served in the U.S. Army as a [counterintelligence](https://www.britannica.com/topic/counterintelligence) agent, but his first experience with combat was on D-Day (June 6, 1944), when he participated in the [Normandy landings](https://www.britannica.com/event/Normandy-Invasion) on [Utah Beach](https://www.britannica.com/place/Utah-Beach). He also fought in the [Battle of the Bulge](https://www.britannica.com/event/Battle-of-the-Bulge) and participated in the liberation of a [concentration camp](https://www.britannica.com/topic/concentration-camp) in Germany.

### How did J.D. Salinger’s experience in World War II influence his writing?

[J.D. Salinger](https://www.britannica.com/biography/J-D-Salinger)’s experience in the U.S. Army during [World War II](https://www.britannica.com/event/World-War-II) influenced many elements in his [short stories](https://www.britannica.com/art/short-story). For example, “For Esmé—with Love and Squalor” (1950) describes a U.S. soldier’s poignant encounter with two British children. “A Perfect Day for Bananafish” (1948) concerns the [suicide](https://www.britannica.com/topic/suicide) of the sensitive, despairing veteran Seymour Glass.

### Why did J.D. Salinger become a recluse?

American author [J.D. Salinger](https://www.britannica.com/biography/J-D-Salinger) (1919–2010) became a recluse after the success of his novel _The Catcher in the Rye_ (1951), seeking to escape fame and preserve his privacy. In 1953 he moved from New York City to Cornish, New Hampshire, and rarely engaged with the media or fans to the end of his life.

**J.D. Salinger** (born January 1, 1919, [Manhattan](https://www.britannica.com/place/Manhattan-New-York-City), [New York](https://www.britannica.com/place/New-York-state), U.S.—died January 27, 2010, Cornish, New Hampshire) was an American writer whose [novel](https://www.britannica.com/art/novel)_The Catcher in the Rye_ (1951) won critical acclaim and devoted admirers, especially among the post-[World War II](https://www.britannica.com/event/World-War-II) generation of college students. His corpus of published works also consists of [short stories](https://www.britannica.com/art/short-story) that were printed in magazines, including _The Saturday Evening Post_, _[Esquire](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Esquire-American-magazine)_, and _[The New Yorker](https://www.britannica.com/topic/The-New-Yorker)_. After the success of _The Catcher in the Rye_, Salinger became a recluse. His last published work was a short story in 1965, but he remained an enormously influential figure in contemporary [American literature](https://www.britannica.com/art/American-literature).

## Early life and education

Salinger was the son of a Jewish father, Sol Salinger, and a Scotch-Irish Christian mother, Miriam Salinger (née Marie Jillich). He had an older sister, Doris. Like [Holden Caulfield](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Holden-Caulfield), the hero of _The Catcher in the Rye_, Salinger grew up in [New York City](https://www.britannica.com/place/New-York-City). He attended public schools until his parents enrolled him in McBurney School, an [exclusive](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/exclusive) Manhattan [prep school](https://www.britannica.com/topic/preparatory-school), in the ninth grade. After he failed (also like Holden), his parents sent him to Valley Forge Military Academy in Pennsylvania, which became the model for Pencey Prep in _The Catcher in the Rye_. At [Valley Forge](https://www.britannica.com/place/Valley-Forge-historical-area) his plans to become a writer solidified; he served as literary editor of the school yearbook. His other activities there included managing the school’s [fencing](https://www.britannica.com/sports/fencing) team—another similarity he shared with Holden Caulfield.

After brief periods at [New York](https://www.britannica.com/topic/New-York-University) and [Columbia](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Columbia-University) universities, Salinger devoted himself entirely to writing, and his stories began to appear in periodicals in 1940. The next year he had a [brief career as a cruise ship entertainment director](https://www.britannica.com/topic/List-of-Day-Jobs-of-Famous-Writers).

## Wartime experiences

During [World War II](https://www.britannica.com/event/World-War-II), J.D. Salinger’s first time in combat was in Normandy on D-Day (June 6, 1944).

In 1942 Salinger was [drafted](https://www.britannica.com/dictionary/drafted) into the U.S. Army. Proficient in French and German, he served as a [counterintelligence](https://www.britannica.com/topic/counterintelligence) agent in the 4th Infantry Division and was tasked with interviewing prisoners-of-war, [Nazi](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Nazi-Party) sympathizers, and military deserters. Two years later Salinger participated in the [Normandy landings](https://www.britannica.com/event/Normandy-Invasion) on [Utah Beach](https://www.britannica.com/place/Utah-Beach) on D-Day (June 6, 1944). It was his first time in combat.

Later, Salinger fought in the [Battle of the Bulge](https://www.britannica.com/event/Battle-of-the-Bulge) and participated in the liberation of the [concentration camp](https://www.britannica.com/topic/concentration-camp) at Kaufering, Germany, a subcamp of [Dachau](https://www.britannica.com/place/Dachau-concentration-camp-Germany). While in Europe he met [Ernest Hemingway](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Ernest-Hemingway), who was working as a war correspondent and encouraged Salinger in his writing. However, the war seriously affected the young writer’s health. For several weeks he was hospitalized while being treated for “[battle fatigue](https://www.britannica.com/science/combat-fatigue)” ([post-traumatic stress disorder](https://www.britannica.com/science/post-traumatic-stress-disorder)). During his recovery he wrote a story titled “I’m Crazy,” which was narrated by a teenage character named Holden Caulfield. It was not the first time Holden appeared in one of Salinger’s stories, but it was the first story in which he served as the narrator. “I’m Crazy” was published in December 1945 in _Collier’s_.

_[(Read about other writers who went to war in Britannica’s article “War Stories.”)](https://www.britannica.com/art/War-Stories-13-Modern-Writers-Who-Served-in-War)_

## Literary fame with _The Catcher in the Rye_ and a life in seclusion

After Salinger’s return to the [United States](https://www.britannica.com/place/United-States) (he was honorably discharged in 1946), his name and writing style became increasingly associated with _[The New Yorker](https://www.britannica.com/topic/The-New-Yorker)_ magazine, which published almost all of his later stories. Some of the best of these made use of his wartime experiences: “For Esmé—with Love and Squalor” (1950) describes a U.S. soldier’s [poignant](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/poignant) encounter with two British children, and “A Perfect Day for Bananafish” (1948) concerns the [suicide](https://www.britannica.com/topic/suicide) of the sensitive, despairing veteran Seymour Glass.

Major critical and popular recognition came with the publication of _The Catcher in the Rye_, whose central character, the sensitive, rebellious Holden Caulfield, relates in authentic teenage [idiom](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/idiom) his flight from the “phony” adult world, his search for innocence and truth, and his final collapse on a psychiatrist’s couch. The humor and colorful language of _The Catcher in the Rye_ place it in the tradition of [Mark Twain](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Mark-Twain)’s _[Adventures of Huckleberry Finn](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Adventures-of-Huckleberry-Finn-novel-by-Twain)_ and the stories of [Ring Lardner](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Ring-Lardner), but its hero, like most of Salinger’s child characters, views his life with an added dimension of [precocious](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/precocious) self-consciousness.

_The Catcher in the Rye_ made Salinger into a literary celebrity. In an attempt to escape fame and recover the loss of his privacy, he moved from New York to Cornish, [New Hampshire](https://www.britannica.com/place/New-Hampshire-state), in 1953 and went into seclusion. To the end of his life Salinger rarely spoke to the media or engaged with his many fans.

For a while, he continued to publish new work. _Nine Stories_ (1953), a selection of Salinger’s short stories, added to his literary reputation. Several pieces in the collection, which includes “A Perfect Day for Bananafish,” feature the siblings of the fictional [Glass family](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Glass-family). In works such as _[Franny and Zooey](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Franny-and-Zooey)_ (1961) and _Raise High the Roof Beam, Carpenters and Seymour: An Introduction_ (1963), the introspective Glass children, influenced by their eldest brother Seymour and his death, navigate questions about [spirituality](https://www.britannica.com/topic/spirituality) and enlightenment. Similar to _The Catcher in the Rye_, all three books were best-sellers.

## Personal life and later years

The reclusive habits of Salinger in his later years made his personal life a matter of speculation among devotees. According to family members, Salinger’s life in seclusion reflected the quest for spiritual enlightenment of his characters in _Raise High the Roof Beam_. He developed interests in [homeopathic](https://www.britannica.com/science/homeopathy) medicine and [acupuncture](https://www.britannica.com/science/acupuncture), Eastern religions such as [Buddhism](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Buddhism) and [Hinduism](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Hinduism), and [Christian Science](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Christian-Science) and [Scientology](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Scientology). Many critics think Salinger’s [esoteric](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/esoteric) interests were fueled by the trauma of his war experiences.

Salinger was married three times. In 1945 he wed Sylvia Welter, a German woman whom he met in Europe and about whom little else is known. Their marriage lasted eight months. In 1955 he married Claire Douglas, a 19-year-old student at Radcliffe College; they had two children, Margaret and Matthew, before divorcing in 1967.

He subsequently had relationships with several other women, including writer Joyce Maynard, an 18-year-old student at [Yale University](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Yale-University). In April 1972 she had published an [essay in _The New York Times Magazine_](https://archive.nytimes.com/www.nytimes.com/books/98/09/13/specials/maynard-mag.html) that had impressed him—or perhaps, her youthful appearance in the essay’s accompanying photograph did. Salinger, then 53 years old, wrote to her, and they began a correspondence that led to Maynard dropping out of school and moving in with him. After 10 months they broke up, and Maynard returned to Yale. In 1998 she published _At Home in the World_, a memoir of their relationship. The following year she auctioned off his letters. Salinger made no public comment, but he privately accused Maynard of [exploiting](https://www.britannica.com/dictionary/exploiting) him.

In the late 1980s Salinger married Colleen O’Neill, a nurse who is believed to have been about 40 years younger than him.

Meanwhile, his small literary output was a subject of controversy among critics. The last work Salinger published during his lifetime was a [novella](https://www.britannica.com/art/novella) titled _Hapworth 16, 1924_, which appeared in _The New Yorker_ in 1965. It concerns the childhood of Seymour Glass and a letter he writes to his family from [summer camp](https://www.britannica.com/topic/summer-camp). In 1997 Salinger consented to a publisher’s plans to release _Hapworth 16, 1924_ as a book, but he suddenly withdrew his support, scuttling its publication.

“It’s clear he wasn’t so crazy about the splashy aspects of publishing on a certain scale…But I don’t think he ever could strike that balance between the public and private worlds of writing and publishing his work.”—Dave Eggers on Salinger, in _The New Yorker_, 2010

In 1974 _The Complete Uncollected Short Stories of J.D. Salinger_, an unauthorized two-volume work of his early pieces, was briefly released to the public, but sales were halted when Salinger filed a lawsuit for [copyright](https://www.britannica.com/topic/copyright) infringement. Salinger also sued to stop the publication of a biography of him by Ian Hamilton and an unauthorized sequel to _The Catcher in the Rye_. The biography was rewritten and published in 1988 under the title _In Search of J.D. Salinger_. The sequel, _60 Years Later: Coming Through the Rye_, by John David California (a pseudonym of the Swedish writer Fredrik Colting), was published in Britain in 2009, but a judge barred its publication in the United States.

Other unauthorized works about Salinger include _Dream Catcher_ (2000), a memoir by his daughter that claimed he had been abusive to his second wife. She also chronicled his esoteric beliefs and wrote that his personal habits included [arcane](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/arcane) health practices such as drinking his own urine. Salinger’s son, however, has disputed his sister’s account.

## Death and legacy

Salinger died of natural causes in 2010 at age 91. After his death his literary agents released a statement that read in part,

> Salinger had remarked that he was in this world but not of it. His body is gone but the family hopes that he is still with those he loves, whether they are religious or historical figures, personal friends or fictional characters.

Three years later David Shields and Shane Salerno published _Salinger_, a best-selling biography that claimed the writer had several unpublished works that would eventually be released. Others in the literary world had also made such claims; Maynard believed Salinger had the manuscripts for at least two novels locked in a safe at his home. Many people speculated that he had written several volumes about the Glass family. However, no new works were forthcoming.

Salinger’s influence on writers of the latter half of the 20th century and early 21st century was immense. His literary voice was characterized by its humor, [irony](https://www.britannica.com/art/irony), and a pitch-perfect use of [colloquial](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/colloquial) speech. Among those whose work he influenced are [Sylvia Plath](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Sylvia-Plath), [Philip Roth](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Philip-Roth), [Harold Brodkey](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Harold-Brodkey), [John Updike](https://www.britannica.com/biography/John-Updike), and [Dave Eggers](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Dave-Eggers). After Salinger’s death, Eggers memorialized him in an [essay in _The New Yorker_](https://www.newyorker.com/books/page-turner/remembering-salinger-dave-eggers). He wrote,

> His is still my favorite [dialogue](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/dialogue), the dialogue that rings truest, that’s at once very naturalistic and musical…The man was an artist, no doubt about it, and his work was always growing in new—darker, stranger, more wonderfully obsessive—directions. And always, no matter where the stories go (or don’t go), his sentences are so beautiful, and so unlike anyone else’s.
