Centers of higher education have been around for hundreds of years, and even millennia in some cases, but not all withstand the test of time. Over the centuries, many of the world’s oldest universities have disbanded, split into autonomous colleges or become modernized beyond all recognition.

The ancient institutions that are here today are significant for their historic legacies and for proving their ability to adapt to modern contexts and remain relevant in a globalized world in spite of intense competition.

Here we cover some of the oldest universities in the world, all of which feature in one of the[QS rankings](https://www.topuniversities.com/university-rankings). Most are located in[Europe](https://www.topuniversities.com/where-to-study/region/europe/guide), due to the particularly impressive number of longstanding and prestigious universities in this region, but there’s also an African representative to consider.

This is not intended to be a list of the 10 oldest universities in order of establishment, but instead highlights 10 of the oldest universities which also have a high international ranking.

## University of Bologna

![Image 30: University of Bologna](https://www.topuniversities.com/sites/default/files/university-of-bologna_0.jpg)

**Location:**[Italy](https://www.topuniversities.com/where-to-study/europe/italy/guide)

**Established in:**1088

The ‘Nourishing Mother of the Studies’ according to its Latin motto, the University of Bologna was founded in 1088 and, having never been out of operation, is widely regarded as the oldest continuously operating university in the Western world. Until relatively modern times, the university only taught doctorate studies, but today it has a diverse range of programs at all levels.

Located in Bologna, Italy, it has an enrolment of over 85,000 students. Famous alumni include three popes, numerous businessmen and several Italian politicians.

See how the University of Bologna ranks in the[**QS World University Rankings®**](https://www.topuniversities.com/world-university-rankings "https://www.topuniversities.com/university-rankings/world-university-rankings/2023")

## University of Oxford

![Image 31: University of Oxford](https://www.topuniversities.com/sites/default/files/university-of-oxford_0.jpg)

**Location:**[United Kingdom](https://www.topuniversities.com/student-info/qs-guides/how-to-study-abroad-in-the-UK)

**Established in:**1096-1167

With an alumni list that includes 28 UK Prime Ministers, 20 Archbishops of Canterbury, 12 saints, multiple Nobel Prize winners and one Sir Stephen Hawking, the[**University of Oxford**](https://www.topuniversities.com/universities/university-oxford/)is as respected as it is old.

While the university’s exact foundation date remains a little vague, evidence of teaching dates as far back as 1096, and some claim it was established even earlier.

The University of Oxford is truly one of the highest-ranked and oldest universities in the world, catering to a student community of over 24,000 and operating the largest university press in the world.

## University of Salamanca

![Image 32: University of Salamanca](https://www.topuniversities.com/sites/default/files/university-of-salamanca.jpg)

**Location:**[Spain](https://www.topuniversities.com/student-info/qs-guides/how-to-study-abroad-in-spain)

**Established in:**1134

The University of Salamanca was founded in 1134 and given the Royal Charter in 1218, making it Spain’s oldest institution, after the now defunct University of Palencia.

Located to the west of Madrid, it was the institution where Christopher Columbus made a case to obtain royal support for his Indies expedition in the late 15 th century.

The University of Salamanca caters to around 26,746 students across its nine campuses.

See how the University of Salamanca ranks in the[**QS World University Rankings®**](https://www.topuniversities.com/world-university-rankings "https://www.topuniversities.com/university-rankings/world-university-rankings/2023")

## University of Paris

![Image 33: Sorbonne University](https://www.topuniversities.com/sites/default/files/university-of-paris_sorbonne.jpg)

**Location:**[France](https://www.topuniversities.com/student-info/qs-guides/how-to-study-abroad-in-france)

**Established in:**1160-1250

Established between 1160 and 1250 in the French capital, the University of Paris, often known as ‘la Sorbonne’, is known to have been one of the first established universities in Europe, although it was suspended from operating between 1793 and 1896, following the French Revolution.

Today, the University of Paris has been dissolved into multiple institutions, some of which have subsequently merged or been reorganised.

[Discover more of the top universities in Paris here](https://www.topuniversities.com/where-to-study/europe/france/paris/top-10-universities-paris).

## University of Cambridge

**Location:**UK

**Established in:**1209

The University of Cambridge was established in 1209 by a group of scholars leaving the University of Oxford due to political conflicts.

Sharing many common traditions,[Oxford and Cambridge](https://www.topuniversities.com/student-info/choosing-university/oxford-or-cambridge)maintain a healthy sense of rivalry, which comes to a head in the famous annual Boat Race event.

## University of Padua

![Image 34: University of Padua](https://www.topuniversities.com/sites/default/files/university-of-padua.jpg)

**Location:**Italy

**Established in:**1222

The University of Padua –Università di Padova or UNIPD – was founded in 1222 (although some evidence puts it before this date) and is one of a number of medieval universities in Italy still operating.

The Università di Padova is notable for its revolutionary early research in astronomy, law, medicine and philosophy.See how the University of Padua ranks in the[**QS World University Rankings®**](https://www.topuniversities.com/world-university-rankings "https://www.topuniversities.com/university-rankings/world-university-rankings/2023")

It now hosts around 62,500 students in the city of Padua, the setting of William Shakespeare’s famous play _The Taming of the Shrew_. In 1545, the Università di Padova established the Botanical Garden of Padova, now one of the oldest academic gardens in the world. It also runs nine museums.

## University of Naples Federico II

![Image 39: University of Naples - Federico II ](https://www.topuniversities.com/sites/default/files/university_of_naples_-_federico_ii.jpg)

**Location:**Italy

**Established in:**1224

Founded in 1224 by Frederick II, emperor of the Holy Roman Empire, the University of Naples - Federico II is located in Naples, Italy’s third-largest city and one of the oldest continuously inhabited cities in the world.

The University of Naples Federico II teaches a wide range of programmes to a student community of around 80,000. Among its most famous historic alumni is the philosopher and theologian Thomas Aquinas.

## University of Siena

![Image 40: University of Siena](https://www.topuniversities.com/sites/default/files/university-of-siena.jpg)

**Location:**Italy

**Established in:**1240

Located in the small city of Siena in the Tuscany region, the University of Siena is another of the oldest universities in the world with a strong global standing.

With enrolment numbers upwards of 20,000, the University of Siena campus comprises almost half of the city’s entire population. The city center itself, also of historic importance, has been declared a UNESCO World Heritage Site and is visited annually by over 163,000 tourists who come for the food, the art, the museums and the medieval heritage.

## University of Coimbra

**Location:**[Portugal](https://www.topuniversities.com/where-to-study/europe/portugal/guide)

![Image 41: University of Coimbra](https://www.topuniversities.com/sites/default/files/university-of-coimbra.jpg)**Established in:**1290

Although originally established in the Portuguese capital in 1290, the University of Coimbra was relocated a number of times by demanding kings, finally ending up in Coimbra, the country’s third-largest urban center and home to much Roman-era history.

With a student community of just over 24,000, the University of Coimbra has been through many radical reforms, and for decades in the 18 th century it was the only operating university in Portugal.

In 2013, the University of Coimbra was added to the UNESCO World Heritage List in recognition of its historical buildings, open courtyard, cultural traditions and stunning city-wide views.

## Al-Azhar University

![Image 42:  Al-Azhar University](https://www.topuniversities.com/sites/default/files/al-azhar-university.jpg)

**Location:**[Egypt](https://www.topuniversities.com/where-to-study/africa/egypt/guide)

**Established in:**970 AD

Scholars differ on whether medieval institutions such as Al-Azhar University should be classified as universities before their modern reorganisation, but we feel it deserves a mention in this list as it was originally established as early as 970 AD in Cairo, Egypt. Originally a ‘madrasa’, teaching students from primary to tertiary level, Al-Azhar University was first known as a center of Islamic learning but has since developed a modern curriculum of secular subjects, ensuring its survival.

Through its time, the school has seen much political instability, most notably in the 12 th century when a new dynasty took power and destroyed over 100,000 texts. In addition to traditional studies, the school also offers programs in business, economics, science, medicine, engineering and agriculture.

Centers of higher education have been around for hundreds of years, and even millennia in some cases, but not all withstand the test of time. Over the centuries, many of the world’s oldest universities have disbanded, split into autonomous colleges or become modernized beyond all recognition.

The ancient institutions that are here today are significant for their historic legacies and for proving their ability to adapt to modern contexts and remain relevant in a globalized world in spite of intense competition.

Here we cover some of the oldest universities in the world, all of which feature in one of the[QS rankings](https://www.topuniversities.com/university-rankings). Most are located in[Europe](https://www.topuniversities.com/where-to-study/region/europe/guide), due to the particularly impressive number of longstanding and prestigious universities in this region, but there’s also an African representative to consider.

This is not intended to be a list of the 10 oldest universities in order of establishment, but instead highlights 10 of the oldest universities which also have a high international ranking.

## University of Bologna

![Image 30: University of Bologna](https://www.topuniversities.com/sites/default/files/university-of-bologna_0.jpg)

**Location:**[Italy](https://www.topuniversities.com/where-to-study/europe/italy/guide)

**Established in:**1088

The ‘Nourishing Mother of the Studies’ according to its Latin motto, the University of Bologna was founded in 1088 and, having never been out of operation, is widely regarded as the oldest continuously operating university in the Western world. Until relatively modern times, the university only taught doctorate studies, but today it has a diverse range of programs at all levels.

Located in Bologna, Italy, it has an enrolment of over 85,000 students. Famous alumni include three popes, numerous businessmen and several Italian politicians.

See how the University of Bologna ranks in the[**QS World University Rankings®**](https://www.topuniversities.com/world-university-rankings "https://www.topuniversities.com/university-rankings/world-university-rankings/2023")

## University of Oxford

![Image 31: University of Oxford](https://www.topuniversities.com/sites/default/files/university-of-oxford_0.jpg)

**Location:**[United Kingdom](https://www.topuniversities.com/student-info/qs-guides/how-to-study-abroad-in-the-UK)

**Established in:**1096-1167

With an alumni list that includes 28 UK Prime Ministers, 20 Archbishops of Canterbury, 12 saints, multiple Nobel Prize winners and one Sir Stephen Hawking, the[**University of Oxford**](https://www.topuniversities.com/universities/university-oxford/)is as respected as it is old.

While the university’s exact foundation date remains a little vague, evidence of teaching dates as far back as 1096, and some claim it was established even earlier.

The University of Oxford is truly one of the highest-ranked and oldest universities in the world, catering to a student community of over 24,000 and operating the largest university press in the world.

## University of Salamanca

![Image 32: University of Salamanca](https://www.topuniversities.com/sites/default/files/university-of-salamanca.jpg)

**Location:**[Spain](https://www.topuniversities.com/student-info/qs-guides/how-to-study-abroad-in-spain)

**Established in:**1134

The University of Salamanca was founded in 1134 and given the Royal Charter in 1218, making it Spain’s oldest institution, after the now defunct University of Palencia.

Located to the west of Madrid, it was the institution where Christopher Columbus made a case to obtain royal support for his Indies expedition in the late 15 th century.

The University of Salamanca caters to around 26,746 students across its nine campuses.

See how the University of Salamanca ranks in the[**QS World University Rankings®**](https://www.topuniversities.com/world-university-rankings "https://www.topuniversities.com/university-rankings/world-university-rankings/2023")

## University of Paris

![Image 33: Sorbonne University](https://www.topuniversities.com/sites/default/files/university-of-paris_sorbonne.jpg)

**Location:**[France](https://www.topuniversities.com/student-info/qs-guides/how-to-study-abroad-in-france)

**Established in:**1160-1250

Established between 1160 and 1250 in the French capital, the University of Paris, often known as ‘la Sorbonne’, is known to have been one of the first established universities in Europe, although it was suspended from operating between 1793 and 1896, following the French Revolution.

Today, the University of Paris has been dissolved into multiple institutions, some of which have subsequently merged or been reorganised.

[Discover more of the top universities in Paris here](https://www.topuniversities.com/where-to-study/europe/france/paris/top-10-universities-paris).

## University of Cambridge

**Location:**UK

**Established in:**1209

The University of Cambridge was established in 1209 by a group of scholars leaving the University of Oxford due to political conflicts.

Sharing many common traditions,[Oxford and Cambridge](https://www.topuniversities.com/student-info/choosing-university/oxford-or-cambridge)maintain a healthy sense of rivalry, which comes to a head in the famous annual Boat Race event.

## University of Padua

![Image 34: University of Padua](https://www.topuniversities.com/sites/default/files/university-of-padua.jpg)

**Location:**Italy

**Established in:**1222

The University of Padua –Università di Padova or UNIPD – was founded in 1222 (although some evidence puts it before this date) and is one of a number of medieval universities in Italy still operating.

The Università di Padova is notable for its revolutionary early research in astronomy, law, medicine and philosophy.See how the University of Padua ranks in the[**QS World University Rankings®**](https://www.topuniversities.com/world-university-rankings "https://www.topuniversities.com/university-rankings/world-university-rankings/2023")

It now hosts around 62,500 students in the city of Padua, the setting of William Shakespeare’s famous play _The Taming of the Shrew_. In 1545, the Università di Padova established the Botanical Garden of Padova, now one of the oldest academic gardens in the world. It also runs nine museums.

## University of Naples Federico II

![Image 39: University of Naples - Federico II ](https://www.topuniversities.com/sites/default/files/university_of_naples_-_federico_ii.jpg)

**Location:**Italy

**Established in:**1224

Founded in 1224 by Frederick II, emperor of the Holy Roman Empire, the University of Naples - Federico II is located in Naples, Italy’s third-largest city and one of the oldest continuously inhabited cities in the world.

The University of Naples Federico II teaches a wide range of programmes to a student community of around 80,000. Among its most famous historic alumni is the philosopher and theologian Thomas Aquinas.

## University of Siena

![Image 40: University of Siena](https://www.topuniversities.com/sites/default/files/university-of-siena.jpg)

**Location:**Italy

**Established in:**1240

Located in the small city of Siena in the Tuscany region, the University of Siena is another of the oldest universities in the world with a strong global standing.

With enrolment numbers upwards of 20,000, the University of Siena campus comprises almost half of the city’s entire population. The city center itself, also of historic importance, has been declared a UNESCO World Heritage Site and is visited annually by over 163,000 tourists who come for the food, the art, the museums and the medieval heritage.

## University of Coimbra

**Location:**[Portugal](https://www.topuniversities.com/where-to-study/europe/portugal/guide)

![Image 41: University of Coimbra](https://www.topuniversities.com/sites/default/files/university-of-coimbra.jpg)**Established in:**1290

Although originally established in the Portuguese capital in 1290, the University of Coimbra was relocated a number of times by demanding kings, finally ending up in Coimbra, the country’s third-largest urban center and home to much Roman-era history.

With a student community of just over 24,000, the University of Coimbra has been through many radical reforms, and for decades in the 18 th century it was the only operating university in Portugal.

In 2013, the University of Coimbra was added to the UNESCO World Heritage List in recognition of its historical buildings, open courtyard, cultural traditions and stunning city-wide views.

## Al-Azhar University

![Image 42:  Al-Azhar University](https://www.topuniversities.com/sites/default/files/al-azhar-university.jpg)

**Location:**[Egypt](https://www.topuniversities.com/where-to-study/africa/egypt/guide)

**Established in:**970 AD

Scholars differ on whether medieval institutions such as Al-Azhar University should be classified as universities before their modern reorganisation, but we feel it deserves a mention in this list as it was originally established as early as 970 AD in Cairo, Egypt. Originally a ‘madrasa’, teaching students from primary to tertiary level, Al-Azhar University was first known as a center of Islamic learning but has since developed a modern curriculum of secular subjects, ensuring its survival.

Through its time, the school has seen much political instability, most notably in the 12 th century when a new dynasty took power and destroyed over 100,000 texts. In addition to traditional studies, the school also offers programs in business, economics, science, medicine, engineering and agriculture.

## About UNA EUROPA

Nine leading European research universities have come together to create a unique alliance – Una Europa. Our universities have been educating Europe for over 1,000 years. Together, we teach almost 450,000 students. Our combined student and staff community surpasses half a million people and our digital learners number in the millions. Una Europa aims to draw on our collective strengths to create a truly European inter-university environment, a University of the Future.

### Our partner universities

#### Freie Universität Berlin

Freie Universität Berlin was founded in 1948 by students and professors as a response to reprisals faced by critical students at the traditional Berlin university, at that time called Universität unter den Linden, which was located in the Soviet sector of the divided city. The US Allies and Berlin politicians approved of the plans for founding a free university. This paved the way for Freie Universität to become an internationally recognized university. The academic ethos of Freie Universität Berlin, based in its founding history, encompasses the three values: Veritas, Justitia, Libertas – truth, justice, freedom.

Visit our [partner's website](https://www.fu-berlin.de/).

#### Alma Mater Studiorum Università di Bologna

Established in 1088, the Alma Mater Studiorum Università di Bologna is the oldest university in the western world. The University of Bologna has a Multicampus structure, with campuses in Bologna and the Romagna region - Cesena, Forlì, Ravenna and Rimini, and permanent headquarters in Buenos Aires since 1998. With a current community of more than 85,000 students, the university is among the largest in Italy. Alma Mater occupies the first place among Italian universities in terms of number of students abroad and is among the top 5 universities in Europe in terms of number of exchange students.

It is the first Italian university for funds received from the Erasmus+ programme and the second in terms of funds received from the European Commission due to the participation of the Horizon2020 research and innovation programme. The University of Bologna is among the top 5 Italian universities in the main international rankings (QS, Shanghai, Times Higher Education, Censis Guide and the Sole 24Ore rankings).

Visit our [partner's website](https://www.unibo.it/it).

#### University of Edinburgh

Founded in 1583, the University of Edinburgh is one of the world’s top universities, consistently ranked in the world top 50, in the Times Higher Education World Rankings, and placed 18th in the 2019 QS World University Rankings. The University’s entrepreneurial and cross-disciplinary culture attracts students and staff from across the globe, creating a unique Edinburgh experience. The University is currently host to 40,000 students from 156 counties. We provide a stimulating working, learning and teaching environment with access to excellent facilities. Previous students include Nobel Prize winning laureates, pioneers and inventors. The University offers a range of ways to study and is the largest provider of online learning in the Russell Group of UK research-intensive universities.

Visit our [partner's website](https://www.ed.ac.uk/).

#### Helsingin yliopisto/ Helsingfors universitet

Helsingin yliopisto/ Helsingfors universitet is the oldest and largest institution of academic education in Finland, an international scientific community of 40,000 students and researchers. In international university rankings, Helsingin yliopisto typically ranks among the top 100. Helsingin yliopisto seeks solutions for global challenges and creates new ways of thinking to better humanity.

Visit our [partner's website](https://www.helsinki.fi/fi).

#### Uniwersytet Jagielloński w Krakowie

Uniwersytet Jagielloński w Krakowie is a leading Polish higher education institution. It is a comprehensive university, where excellence in research is combined with the highest quality education, innovation and responsible social engagement. It is a place where the rich and creative history of one of the oldest universities in Europe blends with state-of-the-art research infrastructure, innovative technology and future-oriented thinking.

The legacy of the Uniwersytet Jagielloński as epitomized by its most famous alumni – Nicolaus Copernicus, Pope John Paul II or the Nobel Prize winner Wisława Szymborska – is best captured by its motto plus ratio quam vis (reason before force). This attitude, immersed in rationality, tolerance and creativity, has formed the history of the Uniwersytet Jagielloński, and continues to shape its future.

Visit our [partner's website](https://www.uj.edu.pl/).

#### KU Leuven

KU Leuven is an autonomous university which was founded in 1425. It was born of and has grown within the Catholic tradition. KU Leuven endeavours to be a place for open discussion of social, philosophical and ethical issues and a critical centre of reflection in and for the Catholic community. The University is research-intensive, internationally oriented, and carries out both fundamental and applied research. It is strongly inter- and multidisciplinary in focus and strives for international excellence. KU Leuven aims to actively participate in public and cultural debate and in the advancement of a knowledge-based society. KU Leuven carries out its academic activities at various campuses, research parks and hospital facilities in close cooperation with the members of the KU Leuven Association and with its hospital partners.

Visit our [partner's website](https://www.kuleuven.be/kuleuven/).

#### Universidad Complutense de Madrid

Universidad Complutense de Madrid dates back to the 13th century. The original Ciudad Universitaria campus was founded in 1927 with the goal of merging education, science and culture. The University is home to over 86,000 students and also has institutions in the city of Pozuelo de Alarcón. The University offers summer courses in the world heritage site of San Lorenzo del Escorial and boasts a number of study abroad programmes with universities located in Europe and the US. The University’s alumni include many famous historians, philosophers, poets and Prime Ministers. Its graduates are given ‘lifelong training’ that furnishes them with professional skills allied to their chosen fields of work and alongside their academic studies.

Visit our [partner's website](https://www.ucm.es/).

#### Université Paris 1 Panthéon-Sorbonne

Founded in 1253, Paris 1 Panthéon-Sorbonne is one of the oldest universities in the world. The policy of Paris 1 Panthéon-Sorbonne is to conduct excellent interdisciplinary research and learning. It is organised around 3 main scientific areas: Economics and Management, Humanities, and Law and Political Sciences. Research performed at the University is renowned on both a national and international level. The University is currently host to 43,000 students and offers degrees partially taught in English, double degrees with international partners and off-campus training sessions. It has close and long-standing ties with 400 universities around the world and is a member of international networks. The overall goal is to provide researchers and students with a unique opportunity to interact with a broad and global network.

Visit our [partner's website](https://www.pantheonsorbonne.fr/).

#### Universiteit Leiden

Universiteit Leiden was founded in 1575 and is one of the leading international research universities in Europe. Universiteit Leiden encompasses seven faculties in Leiden and The Hague. The campus in Leiden is home to the Leiden Law School, Archaeology and Humanities. Sciences, Medicine and Social and Behavioural Sciences are at the Leiden Bio Science Park where they join forces with the business community and the Leiden University Medical Centre (LUMC). The focus in The Hague is on engaging with international organisations and the public sector, and the campus is home to the Faculty of Governance and Global Affairs and Leiden University College.

The motto of Universiteit Leiden is ‘Praesidium Libertatis’, or ‘Bastion of Freedom’. The university has over 7, 100 staff members and 32, 800 students. Universiteit Leiden is ranked amongst the top 100 universities and part of a number of international networks of universities, including the League of European Research Universities (LERU).

Visit our [partner's website](https://www.universiteitleiden.nl/en).

*   **Universität Zürich**

Universität Zürich (UZH) is committed to the free and open pursuit of scholarship and fosters the values of diversity, interdisciplinarity and scientific discourse. With more than 28,000 students, 9,000 staff and more than 800 professors, UZH is Switzerland's largest university.

Founded in 1833, UZH was Europe's first university founded by the will of the people. Research, teaching, continued education and services are the key tasks of UZH. Seven faculties with more than 150 subject areas offer a wide variety of Bachelor's, Master and PhD programmes. In addition, UZH's continuing education programme covers all relevant topics allowing for lifelong learning. UZH communicates with its stakeholders and the general public through a wide range of activities, including a Children's University, a Senior Citizen University and a variety of science policy dialogues. In addition, UZH operates 12 museums accessible to the public.

Visit our[partner's website.](https://www.uzh.ch/en.html)

### Manifesto

**We believe in a university that is...**

1.   not a place, but a body of knowledge, ideas, and values, evolving freely beyond borders, mediums and time.
2.   the home, therefore the responsibility of its community, namely all the people who share and contribute to its ideals.
3.   created by and for society and as such driven to be of relevance, impact and high quality.
4.   an open tradition, using the lessons of the past as a fertile ground to grow solutions for the future.
5.   a mirror of humanity in all its diversity, reflecting cultures and languages, conventions and disruptions.
6.   resolutely independent, shaping its own standards away from the fleeting trends and the impulses of a hasty world.
7.   ready to embrace the challenges of this hasty world, whose fate relies on educated citizens.
8.   a laboratory of the here and now, where creativity and experimentation unlock the hidden potentials of tomorrow.
9.   an intellectual playground, where critical minds can expand to their full aspiration.
10.   a driving influence, transforming education on a wider scale, shaping Europe’s shared future for the better.

### Focus Areas

On the basis of their mission and values, the Una Europa partners have selected five Focus Areas to launch their collaboration. Each fosters multi-disciplinarity and includes most of the studies offered at our universities. The Focus Areas act as initial thematic “glue” that ties our universities together in our mission to create a virtual campus.

**We focus our research on:**

*   **Cultural Heritage**
The rich and diverse Cultural Heritage across the EU shines evidence on the role that universities have played in the creation and cohesion of European identities.

*   **Data Science and Artificial Intelligence**
Data Science and Artificial Intelligence have a pervasive impact on society in all its dimensions, from the way we live our lives and earn our livelihoods to the way we communicate and make decisions.

*   **European Studies**
The study of today’s complex European landscape in a world in flux requires an innovative and cross-cutting approach through which to observe Europe, its challenges, but also its opportunities.

*   **One Health**
One Health is a recent movement promoting networked thinking about health to improve disease detection, prevention and treatment.

*   **Sustainability**
The 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development presents 17 ambitious goals, which integrate economic, social and environmental dimensions.

### Projects

Projects are the catalysts that transform our joint ambition into concrete actions. The projects showcased here are central to Una Europa, aligning with our mission, involving many of our partners and providing numerous opportunities for involvement.

Our projects:

*   Una.Resin
Selected for funding under the European Union's Horizon2020 Framework Programme, Una.Resin will enable Una Europa to develop joint new strategies and transformative collaboration in research and innovation.  
[Learn more about this project](https://www.una-europa.eu/about/una.resin).

*   1Europe
Funded among the first European University pilots selected by the European Commission in June 2019, our 1Europe project will establish a Europe-wide living lab for testing Joint Innovative Formats for education and mobility (JIFs).  
[Learn more about this project](https://www.una-europa.eu/about/1europe-1).

The University offers a range of ways to study and is the largest provider of online learning in the Russell Group of UK research-intensive universities.

Visit our [partner's website](https://www.ed.ac.uk/).

#### Helsingin yliopisto/ Helsingfors universitet

Helsingin yliopisto/ Helsingfors universitet is the oldest and largest institution of academic education in Finland, an international scientific community of 40,000 students and researchers. In international university rankings, Helsingin yliopisto typically ranks among the top 100. Helsingin yliopisto seeks solutions for global challenges and creates new ways of thinking to better humanity.

Visit our [partner's website](https://www.helsinki.fi/fi).

#### Uniwersytet Jagielloński w Krakowie

Uniwersytet Jagielloński w Krakowie is a leading Polish higher education institution. It is a comprehensive university, where excellence in research is combined with the highest quality education, innovation and responsible social engagement. It is a place where the rich and creative history of one of the oldest universities in Europe blends with state-of-the-art research infrastructure, innovative technology and future-oriented thinking.

The legacy of the Uniwersytet Jagielloński as epitomized by its most famous alumni – Nicolaus Copernicus, Pope John Paul II or the Nobel Prize winner Wisława Szymborska – is best captured by its motto plus ratio quam vis (reason before force). This attitude, immersed in rationality, tolerance and creativity, has formed the history of the Uniwersytet Jagielloński, and continues to shape its future.

Visit our [partner's website](https://www.uj.edu.pl/).

#### KU Leuven

KU Leuven is an autonomous university which was founded in 1425. It was born of and has grown within the Catholic tradition. KU Leuven endeavours to be a place for open discussion of social, philosophical and ethical issues and a critical centre of reflection in and for the Catholic community. The University is research-intensive, internationally oriented, and carries out both fundamental and applied research. It is strongly inter- and multidisciplinary in focus and strives for international excellence. KU Leuven aims to actively participate in public and cultural debate and in the advancement of a knowledge-based society. KU Leuven carries out its academic activities at various campuses, research parks and hospital facilities in close cooperation with the members of the KU Leuven Association and with its hospital partners.

Visit our [partner's website](https://www.kuleuven.be/kuleuven/).

#### Universidad Complutense de Madrid

Universidad Complutense de Madrid dates back to the 13th century. The original Ciudad Universitaria campus was founded in 1927 with the goal of merging education, science and culture. The University is home to over 86,000 students and also has institutions in the city of Pozuelo de Alarcón. The University offers summer courses in the world heritage site of San Lorenzo del Escorial and boasts a number of study abroad programmes with universities located in Europe and the US. The University’s alumni include many famous historians, philosophers, poets and Prime Ministers. Its graduates are given ‘lifelong training’ that furnishes them with professional skills allied to their chosen fields of work and alongside their academic studies.

Visit our [partner's website](https://www.ucm.es/).

#### Université Paris 1 Panthéon-Sorbonne

Founded in 1253, Paris 1 Panthéon-Sorbonne is one of the oldest universities in the world. The policy of Paris 1 Panthéon-Sorbonne is to conduct excellent interdisciplinary research and learning. It is organised around 3 main scientific areas: Economics and Management, Humanities, and Law and Political Sciences. Research performed at the University is renowned on both a national and international level. The University is currently host to 43,000 students and offers degrees partially taught in English, double degrees with international partners and off-campus training sessions. It has close and long-standing ties with 400 universities around the world and is a member of international networks. The overall goal is to provide researchers and students with a unique opportunity to interact with a broad and global network.

Visit our [partner's website](https://www.pantheonsorbonne.fr/).

#### Universiteit Leiden

Universiteit Leiden was founded in 1575 and is one of the leading international research universities in Europe. Universiteit Leiden encompasses seven faculties in Leiden and The Hague. The campus in Leiden is home to the Leiden Law School, Archaeology and Humanities. Sciences, Medicine and Social and Behavioural Sciences are at the Leiden Bio Science Park where they join forces with the business community and the Leiden University Medical Centre (LUMC). The focus in The Hague is on engaging with international organisations and the public sector, and the campus is home to the Faculty of Governance and Global Affairs and Leiden University College.

The motto of Universiteit Leiden is ‘Praesidium Libertatis’, or ‘Bastion of Freedom’. The university has over 7, 100 staff members and 32, 800 students. Universiteit Leiden is ranked amongst the top 100 universities and part of a number of international networks of universities, including the League of European Research Universities (LERU).

Visit our [partner's website](https://www.universiteitleiden.nl/en).

Universität Zürich (UZH) is committed to the free and open pursuit of scholarship and fosters the values of diversity, interdisciplinarity and scientific discourse. With more than 28,000 students, 9,000 staff and more than 800 professors, UZH is Switzerland's largest university.

Founded in 1833, UZH was Europe's first university founded by the will of the people. Research, teaching, continued education and services are the key tasks of UZH. Seven faculties with more than 150 subject areas offer a wide variety of Bachelor's, Master and PhD programmes. In addition, UZH's continuing education programme covers all relevant topics allowing for lifelong learning. UZH communicates with its stakeholders and the general public through a wide range of activities, including a Children's University, a Senior Citizen University and a variety of science policy dialogues. ### Manifesto

**We believe in a university that is...**

1.   not a place, but a body of knowledge, ideas, and values, evolving freely beyond borders, mediums and time.
2.   the home, therefore the responsibility of its community, namely all the people who share and contribute to its ideals.
3.   created by and for society and as such driven to be of relevance, impact and high quality.
4.   an open tradition, using the lessons of the past as a fertile ground to grow solutions for the future.
5.   a mirror of humanity in all its diversity, reflecting cultures and languages, conventions and disruptions.
6.   resolutely independent, shaping its own standards away from the fleeting trends and the impulses of a hasty world.
7.   ready to embrace the challenges of this hasty world, whose fate relies on educated citizens.
8.   a laboratory of the here and now, where creativity and experimentation unlock the hidden potentials of tomorrow.
9.   an intellectual playground, where critical minds can expand to their full aspiration.
10.   a driving influence, transforming education on a wider scale, shaping Europe’s shared future for the better.

### Focus Areas

On the basis of their mission and values, the Una Europa partners have selected five Focus Areas to launch their collaboration. Each fosters multi-disciplinarity and includes most of the studies offered at our universities. The Focus Areas act as initial thematic “glue” that ties our universities together in our mission to create a virtual campus.

**We focus our research on:**

*   **Cultural Heritage**
The rich and diverse Cultural Heritage across the EU shines evidence on the role that universities have played in the creation and cohesion of European identities.

*   **Data Science and Artificial Intelligence**
Data Science and Artificial Intelligence have a pervasive impact on society in all its dimensions, from the way we live our lives and earn our livelihoods to the way we communicate and make decisions.

*   **European Studies**
The study of today’s complex European landscape in a world in flux requires an innovative and cross-cutting approach through which to observe Europe, its challenges, but also its opportunities.

*   **One Health**
One Health is a recent movement promoting networked thinking about health to improve disease detection, prevention and treatment.

*   **Sustainability**
The 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development presents 17 ambitious goals, which integrate economic, social and environmental dimensions.

**university**, institution of [higher education](https://www.britannica.com/topic/higher-education), usually comprising a [college](https://www.britannica.com/topic/college-education) of [liberal arts](https://www.britannica.com/topic/liberal-arts) and sciences and graduate and professional schools and having the authority to confer degrees in various fields of study. A university differs from a college in that it is usually larger, has a broader curriculum, and offers graduate and professional degrees ([master’s](https://www.britannica.com/topic/master-degree) and [doctorates](https://www.britannica.com/topic/doctor-degree)), professional degrees, in addition to undergraduate degrees (such as the [bachelor’s degree](https://www.britannica.com/topic/bachelors-degree)). Although universities did not arise in the West until the [Middle Ages](https://www.britannica.com/event/Middle-Ages) in [Europe](https://www.britannica.com/place/Europe), they existed in some parts of [Asia](https://www.britannica.com/place/Asia) and [Africa](https://www.britannica.com/place/Africa) in ancient times.

## Early universities

The modern Western university evolved from the [medieval](https://www.britannica.com/event/Middle-Ages) schools known as _[studia generalia](https://www.britannica.com/topic/studia-generale)_; they were generally recognized places of study open to students from all parts of [Europe](https://www.britannica.com/place/Europe). The earliest _studia_ arose out of efforts to educate clerks and [monks](https://www.britannica.com/topic/monk-monasticism) beyond the level of the cathedral and [monastic](https://www.britannica.com/topic/monasticism) schools. The inclusion of scholars from foreign countries constituted the primary difference between the _studia_ and the schools from which they grew.

[Giovanni d'Andrea at the University of Bologna](https://cdn.britannica.com/00/198100-050-BE97205B/relief-Giovanni-dAndrea-canon-law-students-University.jpg)Sepulchre of Giovanni d'Andrea featuring a relief depicting him, a professor of canon law, lecturing at the University of Bologna, 1348; in the Medieval Civic Museum, Bologna, Italy.(more)

The earliest Western institution that can be called a university was a famous medical school that arose at [Salerno](https://www.britannica.com/place/Salerno-Italy), Italy, in the 9th century and drew students from all over Europe. It remained merely a medical school, however. The first true university in the West was founded at [Bologna](https://www.britannica.com/topic/University-of-Bologna) late in the 11th century. It became a widely respected school of [canon](https://www.britannica.com/topic/canon-law) and [civil law](https://www.britannica.com/topic/civil-law-Romano-Germanic). The first university to arise in northern Europe was the [University of Paris](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Universities-of-Paris-I-XIII), founded between 1150 and 1170. It became noted for its teaching of [theology](https://www.britannica.com/topic/theology), and it served as a model for other universities in northern Europe such as the [University of Oxford](https://www.britannica.com/topic/University-of-Oxford) in England, which was well established by the end of the 12th century. The Universities of Paris and Oxford were composed of colleges, which were actually endowed residence halls for scholars.

These early universities were corporations of students and masters, and they eventually received their charters from [popes](https://www.britannica.com/topic/pope), [emperors](https://www.britannica.com/topic/emperor-title), and [kings](https://www.britannica.com/topic/monarchy). The University of Naples, founded by Emperor [Frederick II](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Frederick-II-Holy-Roman-emperor) (1224), was the first to be established under imperial authority, while the University of Toulouse, founded by Pope [Gregory IX](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Gregory-IX) (1229), was the first to be established by papal decree. These universities were free to govern themselves, provided they taught neither [atheism](https://www.britannica.com/topic/atheism) nor [heresy](https://www.britannica.com/topic/heresy). Students and masters together elected their own rectors (presidents). As the price of independence, however, universities had to finance themselves. So teachers charged fees, and, to assure themselves of a livelihood, they had to please their students. These early universities had no permanent buildings and little corporate property, and they were subject to the loss of dissatisfied students and masters who could migrate to another city and establish a place of study there. The history of the [University of Cambridge](https://www.britannica.com/topic/University-of-Cambridge) began in 1209 when a number of disaffected students moved there from Oxford, and 20 years later Oxford profited by a migration of students from the University of Paris.

[![Image 18: University of Glasgow, Scotland](https://cdn.britannica.com/33/115033-050-5B3A0A5B/Main-Building-University-of-Glasgow-Scot.jpg?w=300)](https://cdn.britannica.com/33/115033-050-5B3A0A5B/Main-Building-University-of-Glasgow-Scot.jpg)

[University of Glasgow, Scotland](https://cdn.britannica.com/33/115033-050-5B3A0A5B/Main-Building-University-of-Glasgow-Scot.jpg)The Main Building, University of Glasgow, Scotland.(more)

From the 13th century on, universities were established in many of the principal cities of Europe. Universities were founded at Montpellier (beginning of the 13th century) and Aix-en-Provence (1409) in France, at [Padua](https://www.britannica.com/topic/University-of-Padua) (1222), [Rome](https://www.britannica.com/topic/University-of-Rome) (1303), and [Florence](https://www.britannica.com/topic/University-of-Florence) (1321) in Italy, at [Salamanca](https://www.britannica.com/topic/University-of-Salamanca) (1218) in Spain, at Prague (1348) and [Vienna](https://www.britannica.com/topic/University-of-Vienna) (1365) in central Europe, at [Heidelberg](https://www.britannica.com/topic/University-of-Heidelberg) (1386), [Leipzig](https://www.britannica.com/topic/University-of-Leipzig) (1409), Freiburg (1457), and [Tübingen](https://www.britannica.com/topic/University-of-Tubingen) (1477) in what is now Germany, at Louvain (1425) in present-day Belgium, and at [Saint Andrews](https://www.britannica.com/topic/University-of-St-Andrews) (1411) and [Glasgow](https://www.britannica.com/topic/University-of-Glasgow) (1451) in Scotland.

Until the end of the 18th century, most Western universities offered a core curriculum based on the seven liberal arts: [grammar](https://www.britannica.com/topic/grammar), [logic](https://www.britannica.com/topic/logic), [rhetoric](https://www.britannica.com/topic/rhetoric), [geometry](https://www.britannica.com/science/geometry), [arithmetic](https://www.britannica.com/science/arithmetic), [astronomy](https://www.britannica.com/science/astronomy), and [music](https://www.britannica.com/art/music). Students then proceeded to study under one of the professional faculties of [medicine](https://www.britannica.com/science/medicine), [law](https://www.britannica.com/topic/law), and theology. Final examinations were grueling, and many students failed.

## Impact of the [Protestant](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Protestantism)[Reformation](https://www.britannica.com/event/Reformation) and the [Counter-Reformation](https://www.britannica.com/event/Counter-Reformation) on European universities

The [Protestant](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Protestantism)[Reformation](https://www.britannica.com/event/Reformation) of the 16th century and the ensuing [Counter-Reformation](https://www.britannica.com/event/Counter-Reformation) affected the universities of Europe in different ways. In the German states, new Protestant universities were founded and older schools were taken over by Protestants, while many [Roman Catholic](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Roman-Catholicism) universities became staunch defenders of the traditional learning associated with the Catholic church. By the 17th century, both Protestant and Catholic universities had become overly devoted to defending correct [religious doctrines](https://www.britannica.com/topic/doctrine) and hence remained resistant to the new interest in [science](https://www.britannica.com/science/science) that had begun to sweep through Europe. The new learning was discouraged, and thus many universities underwent a period of relative decline. New schools continued to be founded during this time, however, including ones at Edinburgh (1583), Leiden (1575), and Strasbourg (university status, 1621).

The first modern university in Europe was that of [Halle](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Martin-Luther-University-of-Halle-Wittenberg), founded by [Lutherans](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Lutheranism) in 1694. This school was one of the first to renounce religious orthodoxy of any kind in favour of rational and objective intellectual inquiry, and it was the first where teachers lectured in [German](https://www.britannica.com/topic/German-language) (i.e., a [vernacular](https://www.britannica.com/topic/vernacular) language) rather than in [Latin](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Latin-language). Halle’s innovations were adopted by the [University of Göttingen](https://www.britannica.com/topic/University-of-Gottingen) (founded 1737) a generation later and subsequently by most German and many American universities.

In the later 18th and 19th centuries [religion](https://www.britannica.com/topic/study-of-religion) was gradually displaced as the dominant force as European universities became institutions of modern learning and research and were secularized in their curriculum and administration. These trends were typified by the [University of Berlin](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Humboldt-University-of-Berlin) (1809), in which laboratory experimentation replaced conjecture; theological, philosophical, and other traditional doctrines were examined with a new rigour and objectivity; and modern standards of [academic freedom](https://www.britannica.com/topic/academic-freedom) were pioneered. The German model of the university as a complex of graduate schools performing advanced research and experimentation proved to have a worldwide influence.

# First universities in the Western Hemisphere

[![Image 23: Princeton University](https://cdn.britannica.com/60/153260-050-226989EA/Firestone-Library-Princeton-University-New-Jersey.jpg?w=300)](https://cdn.britannica.com/60/153260-050-226989EA/Firestone-Library-Princeton-University-New-Jersey.jpg)

[Princeton University](https://cdn.britannica.com/60/153260-050-226989EA/Firestone-Library-Princeton-University-New-Jersey.jpg)Firestone Library, Princeton University, Princeton, New Jersey.(more)

The first universities in the Western Hemisphere were established by the Spaniards: the [University of Santo Domingo](https://www.britannica.com/place/Autonomous-University-of-Santo-Domingo) (1538) in what is now the Dominican Republic and the University of Michoacán (1539) in Mexico. The earliest American institutions of higher learning were the four-year colleges of [Harvard](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Harvard-University) (1636), [William and Mary](https://www.britannica.com/topic/College-of-William-Mary) (1693), [Yale](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Yale-University) (1701), [Princeton](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Princeton-University) (1746), and [King’s College](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Columbia-University) (1754; now [Columbia](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Columbia-University)). Most early [American](https://www.britannica.com/place/United-States) colleges were established by religious denominations, and most eventually evolved into full-fledged universities. One of the oldest universities in Canada is that at [Toronto](https://www.britannica.com/topic/University-of-Toronto), chartered as King’s College in 1827.

[![Image 24: University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, Michigan](https://cdn.britannica.com/42/13442-050-21A811B5/Law-quadrangle-Mich-University-of-Michigan-Ann.jpg?w=300)](https://cdn.britannica.com/42/13442-050-21A811B5/Law-quadrangle-Mich-University-of-Michigan-Ann.jpg)

[University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, Michigan](https://cdn.britannica.com/42/13442-050-21A811B5/Law-quadrangle-Mich-University-of-Michigan-Ann.jpg)Law quadrangle, University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, Michigan.(more)

As the frontier of the United States moved westward, hundreds of new colleges were founded. American colleges and universities tended to imitate German models, seeking to combine the [Prussian](https://www.britannica.com/place/Prussia) ideal of academic freedom with the native tradition of educational opportunity for the many. The growth of such schools in the United States was greatly spurred by the [Morrill Act](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Land-Grant-College-Act-of-1862) of 1862, which granted each state tracts of land with which to finance new agricultural and mechanical schools. Many “[land-grant colleges](https://www.britannica.com/topic/land-grant-university)” arose from this act, and there developed among these the [Massachusetts Institute of Technology](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Massachusetts-Institute-of-Technology) (MIT), [Cornell University](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Cornell-University), and the state universities of Illinois, Wisconsin, and Minnesota.

## Reorganization, secularization, and modernization from the 19th century

Several European countries in the 19th century reorganized and secularized their universities, notably Italy (1870), Spain (1876), and France (1896). Universities in these and other European countries became mostly state-financed. Women began to be admitted to universities in the second half of the 19th century. Meanwhile, universities’ curricula also continued to evolve. The study of modern [languages](https://www.britannica.com/topic/language) and [literatures](https://www.britannica.com/art/literature) was added to, and in many cases supplanted, the traditional study of Latin, [Greek](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Greek-language), and theology. Such sciences as [physics](https://www.britannica.com/science/physics-science), [chemistry](https://www.britannica.com/science/chemistry), [biology](https://www.britannica.com/science/biology), and [engineering](https://www.britannica.com/technology/engineering) achieved a recognized place in curricula, and by the early 20th century the newer disciplines of [economics](https://www.britannica.com/money/economics), [political science](https://www.britannica.com/topic/political-science), [psychology](https://www.britannica.com/science/psychology), and [sociology](https://www.britannica.com/topic/sociology) were also taught.

[![Image 25: University of Bonn](https://cdn.britannica.com/50/30550-050-D5421DBB/University-of-Bonn-palace-city-German.jpg?w=300)](https://cdn.britannica.com/50/30550-050-D5421DBB/University-of-Bonn-palace-city-German.jpg)

[University of Bonn](https://cdn.britannica.com/50/30550-050-D5421DBB/University-of-Bonn-palace-city-German.jpg)The University of Bonn occupies a former palace in the German city. (more)

In the late 19th and 20th centuries Great Britain and France established universities in many of their colonies in South and Southeast [Asia](https://www.britannica.com/place/Asia) and Africa. Most of the independent countries that emerged from these colonies in the mid-20th century expanded their university systems along the lines of their European or American models, often with major technical and economic assistance from former colonial rulers, industrialized countries, and international agencies such as the [World Bank](https://www.britannica.com/topic/World-Bank). Universities in [Japan](https://www.britannica.com/place/Japan), [China](https://www.britannica.com/place/China), and [Russia](https://www.britannica.com/place/Russia) also evolved in response to pressures for modernization. In [India](https://www.britannica.com/place/India) some preindependence universities, such as Banaras Hindu University (1916) and [Rabindranath Tagore](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Rabindranath-Tagore)’s Visva-Bharati (1921), were founded as alternatives to Western educational principles. The state universities of [Moscow](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Moscow-State-University) (1755) and [St. Petersburg](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Saint-Petersburg-State-University) (1819) retained their preeminence in Russia. [Tokyo](https://www.britannica.com/topic/University-of-Tokyo) (1877) and [Kyōto](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Kyoto-University) (1897) universities were the most prestigious ones in Japan, as was [Peking University](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Peking-University) (1898) in China.

## Modern universities

Modern universities may be financed by national, state, or provincial governments, or they may depend largely on tuition fees paid by their students. The typical modern residential university may enroll 30,000 or more students and educate both undergraduates and graduate students in the entire range of the [arts](https://www.britannica.com/art/visual-arts) and [humanities](https://www.britannica.com/topic/humanities), [mathematics](https://www.britannica.com/science/mathematics), the [social sciences](https://www.britannica.com/topic/social-science), the [physical](https://www.britannica.com/science/physical-science), biological, and [earth sciences](https://www.britannica.com/science/Earth-sciences), and various fields of [technology](https://www.britannica.com/technology/technology). Nonresidential, virtual, and open universities, some of which are modeled after Britain’s [Open University](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Open-University-British-education) (1969), may enroll 200,000 or more students, who pursue both degree-credit and noncredit courses of study. Universities are the main providers of graduate-level training in most professional fields.

**university**, institution of [higher education](https://www.britannica.com/topic/higher-education), usually comprising a [college](https://www.britannica.com/topic/college-education) of [liberal arts](https://www.britannica.com/topic/liberal-arts) and sciences and graduate and professional schools and having the authority to confer degrees in various fields of study. A university differs from a college in that it is usually larger, has a broader curriculum, and offers graduate and professional degrees ([master’s](https://www.britannica.com/topic/master-degree) and [doctorates](https://www.britannica.com/topic/doctor-degree)), professional degrees, in addition to undergraduate degrees (such as the [bachelor’s degree](https://www.britannica.com/topic/bachelors-degree)). Although universities did not arise in the West until the [Middle Ages](https://www.britannica.com/event/Middle-Ages) in [Europe](https://www.britannica.com/place/Europe), they existed in some parts of [Asia](https://www.britannica.com/place/Asia) and [Africa](https://www.britannica.com/place/Africa) in ancient times.

## Early universities

The modern Western university evolved from the [medieval](https://www.britannica.com/event/Middle-Ages) schools known as _[studia generalia](https://www.britannica.com/topic/studia-generale)_; they were generally recognized places of study open to students from all parts of [Europe](https://www.britannica.com/place/Europe). The earliest _studia_ arose out of efforts to educate clerks and [monks](https://www.britannica.com/topic/monk-monasticism) beyond the level of the cathedral and [monastic](https://www.britannica.com/topic/monasticism) schools. The inclusion of scholars from foreign countries constituted the primary difference between the _studia_ and the schools from which they grew.

[![Image 13: Giovanni d'Andrea at the University of Bologna](https://cdn.britannica.com/00/198100-050-BE97205B/relief-Giovanni-dAndrea-canon-law-students-University.jpg?w=300)](https://cdn.britannica.com/00/198100-050-BE97205B/relief-Giovanni-dAndrea-canon-law-students-University.jpg)

[Giovanni d'Andrea at the University of Bologna](https://cdn.britannica.com/00/198100-050-BE97205B/relief-Giovanni-dAndrea-canon-law-students-University.jpg)Sepulchre of Giovanni d'Andrea featuring a relief depicting him, a professor of canon law, lecturing at the University of Bologna, 1348; in the Medieval Civic Museum, Bologna, Italy.(more)

The earliest Western institution that can be called a university was a famous medical school that arose at [Salerno](https://www.britannica.com/place/Salerno-Italy), Italy, in the 9th century and drew students from all over Europe. It remained merely a medical school, however. The first true university in the West was founded at [Bologna](https://www.britannica.com/topic/University-of-Bologna) late in the 11th century. It became a widely respected school of [canon](https://www.britannica.com/topic/canon-law) and [civil law](https://www.britannica.com/topic/civil-law-Romano-Germanic). The first university to arise in northern Europe was the [University of Paris](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Universities-of-Paris-I-XIII), founded between 1150 and 1170. It became noted for its teaching of [theology](https://www.britannica.com/topic/theology), and it served as a model for other universities in northern Europe such as the [University of Oxford](https://www.britannica.com/topic/University-of-Oxford) in England, which was well established by the end of the 12th century. The Universities of Paris and Oxford were composed of colleges, which were actually endowed residence halls for scholars.

These early universities were corporations of students and masters, and they eventually received their charters from [popes](https://www.britannica.com/topic/pope), [emperors](https://www.britannica.com/topic/emperor-title), and [kings](https://www.britannica.com/topic/monarchy). The University of Naples, founded by Emperor [Frederick II](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Frederick-II-Holy-Roman-emperor) (1224), was the first to be established under imperial authority, while the University of Toulouse, founded by Pope [Gregory IX](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Gregory-IX) (1229), was the first to be established by papal decree. These universities were free to govern themselves, provided they taught neither [atheism](https://www.britannica.com/topic/atheism) nor [heresy](https://www.britannica.com/topic/heresy). Students and masters together elected their own rectors (presidents). As the price of independence, however, universities had to finance themselves. So teachers charged fees, and, to assure themselves of a livelihood, they had to please their students. These early universities had no permanent buildings and little corporate property, and they were subject to the loss of dissatisfied students and masters who could migrate to another city and establish a place of study there. The history of the [University of Cambridge](https://www.britannica.com/topic/University-of-Cambridge) began in 1209 when a number of disaffected students moved there from Oxford, and 20 years later Oxford profited by a migration of students from the University of Paris.

[University of Glasgow, Scotland](https://cdn.britannica.com/33/115033-050-5B3A0A5B/Main-Building-University-of-Glasgow-Scot.jpg)The Main Building, University of Glasgow, Scotland.(more)

From the 13th century on, universities were established in many of the principal cities of Europe. Universities were founded at Montpellier (beginning of the 13th century) and Aix-en-Provence (1409) in France, at [Padua](https://www.britannica.com/topic/University-of-Padua) (1222), [Rome](https://www.britannica.com/topic/University-of-Rome) (1303), and [Florence](https://www.britannica.com/topic/University-of-Florence) (1321) in Italy, at [Salamanca](https://www.britannica.com/topic/University-of-Salamanca) (1218) in Spain, at Prague (1348) and [Vienna](https://www.britannica.com/topic/University-of-Vienna) (1365) in central Europe, at [Heidelberg](https://www.britannica.com/topic/University-of-Heidelberg) (1386), [Leipzig](https://www.britannica.com/topic/University-of-Leipzig) (1409), Freiburg (1457), and [Tübingen](https://www.britannica.com/topic/University-of-Tubingen) (1477) in what is now Germany, at Louvain (1425) in present-day Belgium, and at [Saint Andrews](https://www.britannica.com/topic/University-of-St-Andrews) (1411) and [Glasgow](https://www.britannica.com/topic/University-of-Glasgow) (1451) in Scotland.

Until the end of the 18th century, most Western universities offered a core curriculum based on the seven liberal arts: [grammar](https://www.britannica.com/topic/grammar), [logic](https://www.britannica.com/topic/logic), [rhetoric](https://www.britannica.com/topic/rhetoric), [geometry](https://www.britannica.com/science/geometry), [arithmetic](https://www.britannica.com/science/arithmetic), [astronomy](https://www.britannica.com/science/astronomy), and [music](https://www.britannica.com/art/music). Students then proceeded to study under one of the professional faculties of [medicine](https://www.britannica.com/science/medicine), [law](https://www.britannica.com/topic/law), and theology. Final examinations were grueling, and many students failed.

## Impact of the [Protestant](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Protestantism)[Reformation](https://www.britannica.com/event/Reformation) and the [Counter-Reformation](https://www.britannica.com/event/Counter-Reformation) on European universities

The [Protestant](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Protestantism)[Reformation](https://www.britannica.com/event/Reformation) of the 16th century and the ensuing [Counter-Reformation](https://www.britannica.com/event/Counter-Reformation) affected the universities of Europe in different ways. In the German states, new Protestant universities were founded and older schools were taken over by Protestants, while many [Roman Catholic](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Roman-Catholicism) universities became staunch defenders of the traditional learning associated with the Catholic church. By the 17th century, both Protestant and Catholic universities had become overly devoted to defending correct [religious doctrines](https://www.britannica.com/topic/doctrine) and hence remained resistant to the new interest in [science](https://www.britannica.com/science/science) that had begun to sweep through Europe. The new learning was discouraged, and thus many universities underwent a period of relative decline. New schools continued to be founded during this time, however, including ones at Edinburgh (1583), Leiden (1575), and Strasbourg (university status, 1621).

The first modern university in Europe was that of [Halle](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Martin-Luther-University-of-Halle-Wittenberg), founded by [Lutherans](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Lutheranism) in 1694. This school was one of the first to renounce religious orthodoxy of any kind in favour of rational and objective intellectual inquiry, and it was the first where teachers lectured in [German](https://www.britannica.com/topic/German-language) (i.e., a [vernacular](https://www.britannica.com/topic/vernacular) language) rather than in [Latin](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Latin-language). Halle’s innovations were adopted by the [University of Göttingen](https://www.britannica.com/topic/University-of-Gottingen) (founded 1737) a generation later and subsequently by most German and many American universities.

In the later 18th and 19th centuries [religion](https://www.britannica.com/topic/study-of-religion) was gradually displaced as the dominant force as European universities became institutions of modern learning and research and were secularized in their curriculum and administration. These trends were typified by the [University of Berlin](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Humboldt-University-of-Berlin) (1809), in which laboratory experimentation replaced conjecture; theological, philosophical, and other traditional doctrines were examined with a new rigour and objectivity; and modern standards of [academic freedom](https://www.britannica.com/topic/academic-freedom) were pioneered. The German model of the university as a complex of graduate schools performing advanced research and experimentation proved to have a worldwide influence.

# First universities in the Western Hemisphere

[![Image 23: Princeton University](https://cdn.britannica.com/60/153260-050-226989EA/Firestone-Library-Princeton-University-New-Jersey.jpg?w=300)](https://cdn.britannica.com/60/153260-050-226989EA/Firestone-Library-Princeton-University-New-Jersey.jpg)

[Princeton University](https://cdn.britannica.com/60/153260-050-226989EA/Firestone-Library-Princeton-University-New-Jersey.jpg)Firestone Library, Princeton University, Princeton, New Jersey.(more)

The first universities in the Western Hemisphere were established by the Spaniards: the [University of Santo Domingo](https://www.britannica.com/place/Autonomous-University-of-Santo-Domingo) (1538) in what is now the Dominican Republic and the University of Michoacán (1539) in Mexico. The earliest American institutions of higher learning were the four-year colleges of [Harvard](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Harvard-University) (1636), [William and Mary](https://www.britannica.com/topic/College-of-William-Mary) (1693), [Yale](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Yale-University) (1701), [Princeton](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Princeton-University) (1746), and [King’s College](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Columbia-University) (1754; now [Columbia](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Columbia-University)). Most early [American](https://www.britannica.com/place/United-States) colleges were established by religious denominations, and most eventually evolved into full-fledged universities. One of the oldest universities in Canada is that at [Toronto](https://www.britannica.com/topic/University-of-Toronto), chartered as King’s College in 1827.

[University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, Michigan](https://cdn.britannica.com/42/13442-050-21A811B5/Law-quadrangle-Mich-University-of-Michigan-Ann.jpg)Law quadrangle, University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, Michigan.(more)

As the frontier of the United States moved westward, hundreds of new colleges were founded. American colleges and universities tended to imitate German models, seeking to combine the [Prussian](https://www.britannica.com/place/Prussia) ideal of academic freedom with the native tradition of educational opportunity for the many. The growth of such schools in the United States was greatly spurred by the [Morrill Act](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Land-Grant-College-Act-of-1862) of 1862, which granted each state tracts of land with which to finance new agricultural and mechanical schools. Many “[land-grant colleges](https://www.britannica.com/topic/land-grant-university)” arose from this act, and there developed among these the [Massachusetts Institute of Technology](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Massachusetts-Institute-of-Technology) (MIT), [Cornell University](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Cornell-University), and the state universities of Illinois, Wisconsin, and Minnesota.

## Reorganization, secularization, and modernization from the 19th century

Several European countries in the 19th century reorganized and secularized their universities, notably Italy (1870), Spain (1876), and France (1896). Universities in these and other European countries became mostly state-financed. Women began to be admitted to universities in the second half of the 19th century. Meanwhile, universities’ curricula also continued to evolve. The study of modern [languages](https://www.britannica.com/topic/language) and [literatures](https://www.britannica.com/art/literature) was added to, and in many cases supplanted, the traditional study of Latin, [Greek](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Greek-language), and theology. Such sciences as [physics](https://www.britannica.com/science/physics-science), [chemistry](https://www.britannica.com/science/chemistry), [biology](https://www.britannica.com/science/biology), and [engineering](https://www.britannica.com/technology/engineering) achieved a recognized place in curricula, and by the early 20th century the newer disciplines of [economics](https://www.britannica.com/money/economics), [political science](https://www.britannica.com/topic/political-science), [psychology](https://www.britannica.com/science/psychology), and [sociology](https://www.britannica.com/topic/sociology) were also taught.

[![Image 25: University of Bonn](https://cdn.britannica.com/50/30550-050-D5421DBB/University-of-Bonn-palace-city-German.jpg?w=300)](https://cdn.britannica.com/50/30550-050-D5421DBB/University-of-Bonn-palace-city-German.jpg)

[University of Bonn](https://cdn.britannica.com/50/30550-050-D5421DBB/University-of-Bonn-palace-city-German.jpg)The University of Bonn occupies a former palace in the German city. (more)

In the late 19th and 20th centuries Great Britain and France established universities in many of their colonies in South and Southeast [Asia](https://www.britannica.com/place/Asia) and Africa. Most of the independent countries that emerged from these colonies in the mid-20th century expanded their university systems along the lines of their European or American models, often with major technical and economic assistance from former colonial rulers, industrialized countries, and international agencies such as the [World Bank](https://www.britannica.com/topic/World-Bank). Universities in [Japan](https://www.britannica.com/place/Japan), [China](https://www.britannica.com/place/China), and [Russia](https://www.britannica.com/place/Russia) also evolved in response to pressures for modernization. In [India](https://www.britannica.com/place/India) some preindependence universities, such as Banaras Hindu University (1916) and [Rabindranath Tagore](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Rabindranath-Tagore)’s Visva-Bharati (1921), were founded as alternatives to Western educational principles. The state universities of [Moscow](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Moscow-State-University) (1755) and [St. Petersburg](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Saint-Petersburg-State-University) (1819) retained their preeminence in Russia. [Tokyo](https://www.britannica.com/topic/University-of-Tokyo) (1877) and [Kyōto](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Kyoto-University) (1897) universities were the most prestigious ones in Japan, as was [Peking University](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Peking-University) (1898) in China.

## Modern universities

Modern universities may be financed by national, state, or provincial governments, or they may depend largely on tuition fees paid by their students. The typical modern residential university may enroll 30,000 or more students and educate both undergraduates and graduate students in the entire range of the [arts](https://www.britannica.com/art/visual-arts) and [humanities](https://www.britannica.com/topic/humanities), [mathematics](https://www.britannica.com/science/mathematics), the [social sciences](https://www.britannica.com/topic/social-science), the [physical](https://www.britannica.com/science/physical-science), biological, and [earth sciences](https://www.britannica.com/science/Earth-sciences), and various fields of [technology](https://www.britannica.com/technology/technology). Nonresidential, virtual, and open universities, some of which are modeled after Britain’s [Open University](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Open-University-British-education) (1969), may enroll 200,000 or more students, who pursue both degree-credit and noncredit courses of study. Universities are the main providers of graduate-level training in most professional fields.
